textbook_title: The Science of the Built Environment

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Which description best defines the built environment?

options.A: The collection of all structures that enclose a roof and walls, excluding roads, utilities, parks, and open spaces
options.B: The set of natural landscapes and ecosystems that surround a city and supply it with water and energy
options.C: Every human-made space where people live, work, and move, including buildings, infrastructure, and open spaces
options.D: The group of professionals and firms that design and construct buildings in a given region

questions.explanation: The built environment spans buildings plus the roads, utilities, and open spaces that connect them, which is why it differs from the natural environment even though the two exchange energy, water, and materials. Restricting it to enclosed structures leaves out infrastructure, and describing the professionals who make it confuses the environment with the construction industry.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what distinguishes a building from other human-made structures such as bridges, towers, and dams?

options.A: A building is always supported by a steel or concrete frame
options.B: A building is enclosed and roofed to shelter people, activities, or goods
options.C: A building is the only structure that must carry gravity and wind loads
options.D: A building is the only structure that requires a permit before construction

questions.explanation: A building is an enclosed, roofed structure that shelters people, activities, or goods. Bridges and dams carry loads too, but they do not enclose usable interior space, so they fall under different standards. Frame material does not define a building, and carrying load is shared by every structure, so neither can be the distinguishing feature.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why does a designer select concrete for a foundation wall against wet soil but dimensional lumber for a small house's floor structure?

options.A: Each material is chosen for the job it must do, and no single material is best at every task
options.B: Concrete is always stronger than lumber, so it is used wherever load must be carried
options.C: Lumber cannot carry any load once it is placed in contact with the ground
options.D: Building codes require concrete below grade and lumber above grade in every building

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that materials are chosen for a job. Concrete resists moisture and is strong in compression, which suits a buried wall, while lumber is light, inexpensive, and easy to install, which suits a floor. Choosing the single strongest material everywhere ignores trade-offs in cost, weight, durability, and moisture behavior.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the construction industry?

options.A: A single group of general contractors that builds every project from start to finish without subcontractors
options.B: It is a government agency that reviews plans and inspects work for code compliance
options.C: It is the set of manufacturers that supply materials and products to building sites
options.D: A network of firms and professionals that plan, design, build, and maintain the built environment

questions.explanation: The construction industry is a large, fragmented network of owners, architects, engineers, contractors, subcontractors, building officials, and suppliers. Describing it as only contractors, only the building official, or only suppliers names a single participant rather than the whole network of people who plan, design, build, and maintain buildings.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why must designers from every discipline coordinate when one building system is changed?

options.A: Each system is built by the same crew, so a change requires rescheduling that crew
options.B: Building codes treat the six systems as a single system for permitting purposes
options.C: Changing a system always requires a new permit from the building official
options.D: The six systems are interdependent, so a change in one ripples into the others

questions.explanation: Systems are interdependent: the enclosure determines how big the mechanical system must be, and mechanical and electrical runs need openings through the structure. The leaky-wall example shows one defect touching four systems. Systems are usually built by different trades, and permits are not the reason designers coordinate.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A framing note reads "Provide a double header over the window opening, bearing on jack studs at each side." What should the framer build?

options.A: A single horizontal board below the window that rests on the floor
options.B: A two-piece beam above the opening resting on short vertical studs at each side
options.C: Two full-height studs placed in front of the glass at each side, with no horizontal member above
options.D: A pair of diagonal braces that connect the window frame to the roof

questions.explanation: A header is a horizontal member that spans an opening, "double" means two pieces, "bearing" means resting on something, and jack studs are the short vertical members that support the header. Together the note describes a two-piece beam carrying loads around the opening instead of through the glass.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A length is written 10'-6" on a drawing. What is it in decimal feet for an engineering calculation?
questions.explanation: To convert feet-inches to decimal feet, divide the inches by 12 and add the result to the feet: 6 / 12 = 0.5, so the length is 10.5 ft. The mistake of writing 10.6 treats inches as tenths of a foot. The result 10.06 comes from dividing by 100 instead of 12, and 11.0 rounds the inches up to a whole foot.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A wall measures 3 in on a plan drawn at 1/4" = 1'-0". What is its real length?

options.A: 12 ft
options.C: 3 ft
options.D: 24 ft

questions.explanation: At 1/4" = 1'-0" the scale is 0.25 in per foot, so the real length is 3 / 0.25 = 12 ft. The answer 0.75 ft comes from multiplying instead of dividing, 3 ft ignores the scale entirely, and 24 ft would result from using 1/8" = 1'-0". Always divide the drawn length by the scale in inches per foot.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why are construction drawings organized into disciplines with letter prefixes such as A, S, M, P, and E?

options.A: So each sheet can be located quickly and cross-referenced by trade within a large set
options.B: So each discipline can use a different scale without having to state it on each sheet
options.C: So the building official can approve each discipline in a separate permit
options.D: So specifications can be removed from the drawings and issued separately

questions.explanation: Drawings are the main way a design is communicated to builders. Letter prefixes group sheets by discipline (architectural, structural, mechanical, plumbing, electrical), and numbered, titled, cross-referenced sheets let each trade find its work. Sheets still must state their scale, and the prefixes have nothing to do with permit approvals or specifications.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Which difference between drawings and specifications is correct?

options.A: Drawings state the quality of materials and the standards they meet, while specifications show their locations
options.B: Drawings show where and how big, while specifications state what quality and by what standard
options.C: Drawings and specifications convey the same information in different formats
options.D: Drawings govern the work, while specifications are advisory only

questions.explanation: A drawing may show a 4 in slab, while the specification adds the required strength, air entrainment, and curing. Neither document tells the builder everything alone. They are complementary, not duplicates, and when they appear to disagree the contract documents state which governs, so the builder should ask instead of guessing.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: On what basis are buildings classified into building types, also called occupancy?

options.A: What material the frame is made from
options.B: How tall the building is
options.C: Who owns the building
options.D: What people do in the building

questions.explanation: Buildings are grouped by what people do in them, a classification called building types or occupancy. The type controls which code provisions apply, how many exits are required, and how much fire resistance is needed. Frame material, height, and ownership may influence design, but they are not the basis of the occupancy classification.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A plan view is best described as which of the following?

options.A: A view of a building face seen straight on without perspective
options.B: A view of an imaginary vertical cut through the building that shows the layers of walls, floors, and roofs
options.C: A view from directly above a horizontal cut through a building, about four feet above the floor
options.D: An enlarged view of a small joint drawn at a large scale

questions.explanation: A plan is a horizontal cut seen from above and answers the question "what is where?" It shows walls, doors, windows, and room layouts. The straight-on face view is an elevation, the vertical cut is a section, and the enlarged joint view is a detail.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why do most Minnesota residential buildings use wood framing?

options.A: Wood framing is the only material allowed by code for buildings where people sleep in Minnesota
options.B: Wood framing offers low cost and fast construction for buildings where people live
options.C: Wood framing resists fire better than steel or concrete frames
options.D: Wood framing needs no protection from moisture in cold climates

questions.explanation: Residential construction covers buildings where people live and is the largest sector by number of projects. Wood framing dominates because of its cost and speed. It is not the only code-permitted option, wood does not outperform steel or concrete in fire resistance, and wood absorbs moisture, so moisture protection remains necessary.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A designer is working on an office building and a hotel. Which description of commercial construction fits these projects?

options.A: Buildings for business and trade, which typically use steel or concrete frames at larger sizes
options.B: Buildings for housing, which are mostly built with wood framing and are the largest sector
options.C: Buildings for processing and storage, where heavy floor loads dominate the design
options.D: Buildings for vulnerable occupants, where life-safety requirements are strictest

questions.explanation: Commercial construction covers offices, shops, restaurants, and hotels, with design emphasis on flexibility and appearance. The housing description matches residential, the heavy-floor-load description matches industrial, and the vulnerable-occupant description matches institutional construction. Matching the use to the right category is how the type is determined.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: A company plans a warehouse with large open floor areas and heavy equipment. Which design emphasis will dominate the structural design?

options.A: Comfort, cost, and construction speed
options.B: Appearance and flexibility for tenants
options.C: Heavy floor loads and large spans
options.D: Life safety for unfamiliar or vulnerable occupants

questions.explanation: Industrial construction covers factories, warehouses, and processing plants where large open floor areas, heavy floor loads, and process equipment dominate the design. Comfort and speed emphasize residential work, appearance and flexibility are commercial priorities, and extra life-safety attention marks institutional buildings such as schools and hospitals.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why are life-safety requirements stricter for institutional buildings such as schools and hospitals?

options.A: Institutional buildings are always taller than other building types
options.B: Institutional buildings use more combustible materials than other types
options.C: Institutional buildings are owned by government and exempt from cost limits
options.D: Occupants are often vulnerable or unfamiliar with the building

questions.explanation: Institutional construction covers schools, hospitals, government buildings, and places of worship. Its occupants may be children, patients, or visitors who cannot easily help themselves or know the exits, so the code raises life-safety requirements. Height, combustibility, and ownership are not the reason for the stricter provisions.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Which question does an elevation answer?

options.A: What is located where on the floor?
options.B: How are the layers of the wall connected at the foundation?
options.C: What are the sizes of every door in the building?
options.D: What does the building face look like, and how tall is it?

questions.explanation: An elevation is a straight-on view of a building face or interior wall without perspective. It shows heights, window and door positions, and exterior materials. The location question belongs to the plan, the layer and connection question to the section or detail, and the door sizes to a schedule.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why is a section the view used to show floor-to-floor heights and how roof and wall layers fit together?

options.A: It shows the building from directly above, so every wall is visible at once
options.B: It shows an imaginary vertical cut, so the interior is revealed as if the building were sliced open
options.C: It shows a table of repeated items, so every layer is listed by mark number
options.D: It shows the exterior face straight on, so all heights are measured from outside the building without cutting

questions.explanation: A section is a vertical cut through the building. Because the cut exposes the interior, it reveals vertical relationships such as foundation depth and the layering of walls and roofs. The view from above is a plan, the table is a schedule, and the straight-on exterior view is an elevation.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why do many building-science failures trace back to details rather than to overall plans?

options.A: A detail specifies how a joint is built, so poor drawing or building of it fails at the connection
options.B: A detail is drawn at a small scale, so dimensions on it are often misread
options.C: A detail replaces the specification entirely, so the quality requirements are missing from the sheets
options.D: A detail is only drawn for exterior walls, so interior joints are never checked

questions.explanation: Details are enlarged views, such as 3" = 1'-0", where the construction of a joint is specified. Failures like leaks and air gaps usually occur at connections between components, so a poorly drawn or poorly built detail is a common cause. Details use large scales, do not replace specifications, and are drawn for many kinds of joints.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: On a floor plan a door is shown only as the tag "D5." Where should a builder look to find that door's width, height, material, and fire rating?

options.A: In the elevation, which shows every door's fire rating directly
options.B: In the symbol legend, which explains the tag
options.C: In the door schedule, which lists each door by mark number
options.D: In the title block of the plan sheet

questions.explanation: A schedule is a table that lists repeated items with their sizes and properties, so drawings can show only the mark and avoid clutter. The door schedule links tag D5 to a row of specifics. The symbol legend explains what symbols mean, and the title block holds sheet information, not the properties of individual doors.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Why should a builder read a drawing set's symbol legend and abbreviation list before reading its sheets?

options.A: Conventions vary among firms, so each set defines its own shorthand
options.B: Abbreviations are legal only when they also appear on the title block of each sheet
options.C: Symbols and abbreviations replace dimensions on the sheets
options.D: The legend lists the code sections that apply to each sheet

questions.explanation: Symbols and abbreviations such as TYP, EQ, and GWB save space, but conventions vary among firms, so each set includes a legend and abbreviation list to define them. Reading these first prevents misinterpretation. They do not replace dimensions and are not a list of code sections.

questions.chapter: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
questions.question_text: Which description best defines building science?

options.A: The set of rules that classify buildings by occupancy and control permits
options.B: The craft of reading drawings and specifications to understand what each trade must build for a project
options.C: The study of how the construction industry is organized into trades
options.D: The applied discipline that explains how buildings carry load, move heat and moisture, and age

questions.explanation: Building science draws on physics, materials science, and engineering to link design and construction choices to performance during occupancy. That is why the book treats forces, heat, and moisture before specific construction systems. Occupancy rules, drawing interpretation, and industry organization are important topics, but they are not what the discipline explains.

questions.question_text: Why is the design process described as both iterative and convergent?

options.A: The team repeats the same drawings until the owner approves, and each decision adds new alternatives
options.B: The team repeats a define, generate, evaluate, and select cycle at finer detail, and each decision removes options
options.C: The team designs each system once in sequence, and every system converges on the same material
options.D: The team revises drawings only after construction starts, and each revision lowers the cost of the finished work

questions.explanation: No one can pick the best answer on the first pass, so the team cycles through define, generate, evaluate, and select at progressively finer levels, from site placement down to a single breaker. It is convergent because each choice, such as a wood-framed roof, narrows the options for ceilings, ducts, and lighting. Repetition alone would not make it convergent.

questions.question_text: Which three flows must the contractor manage simultaneously during the construction process?

options.A: Materials, labor, and information
options.B: Drawings, permits, and inspections
options.C: Design, bidding, and payment
options.D: Owners, architects, and engineers

questions.explanation: The construction process turns documents into a building, and the contractor must coordinate materials (ordered and delivered on time), labor (the right trades in the right order), and information (current drawings and answers). Drawings, permits, inspections, bidding, and payment all matter, but they are not the three flows, and owners and designers are participants, not flows.

questions.question_text: What do project phases accomplish for the owner and the team?

options.A: Each phase is completed by a different contractor who is chosen through competitive bidding for that phase
options.B: Each phase allows earlier decisions to be reversed at no cost to the owner
options.C: Each phase produces defined deliverables and ends with an owner approval, called a phase gate
options.D: Each phase combines design and construction so that work overlaps without approvals

questions.explanation: The standard phases answer different questions, produce defined deliverables, and end with an owner approval before the next phase begins, which protects everyone from building on unconfirmed decisions. Phases are not tied to separate contractors, and reversing early decisions gets more expensive as the project proceeds, so approvals matter most before physical work begins.

questions.question_text: A program lists 4,200 ft² of net area and the owner expects a building efficiency of 0.70. What gross area should the team plan for?
questions.explanation: Gross area equals net area divided by efficiency: 4,200 / 0.70 = 6,000 ft². Multiplying (2,940) inverts the relationship, using the net area alone (4,200) forgets that corridors, walls, and shafts are not part of any room, and simply adding 30 percent (5,460) is not the same as dividing by the efficiency ratio.

questions.question_text: What does the architect explore during schematic design?

options.A: The final dimensions, product models, and installation details for every system
options.B: The competitive prices that contractors offer for the work described in the finished drawings and specifications
options.C: The written approval that allows the owner to occupy the finished building
options.D: The overall form of the building: site placement, shape, height, and room arrangement

questions.explanation: Schematic design compares a few genuinely different options for where the building sits, its shape and height, and how rooms are arranged. Deliverables are a site plan, preliminary floor plans, rough elevations, and a preliminary estimate. Fixing dimensions and products belongs to later phases, pricing belongs to bidding, and occupancy approval belongs to closeout.

questions.question_text: Why is the end of design development sometimes called a design freeze?

options.A: After owner approval, the building official stops reviewing any change to the design for the building permit
options.B: After owner approval, changes become costly because the next phase turns each decision into detailed drawings
options.C: After owner approval, the contractor takes over responsibility for all design decisions
options.D: After owner approval, the design team may no longer coordinate with other disciplines

questions.explanation: Design development settles how the building will be built: systems are chosen and sized, materials selected, and dimensions fixed. Because construction documents will build on every decision, later changes ripple across many sheets and cost much more. The term describes cost and effort, not a legal ban on review, a transfer of design responsibility, or an end to coordination.

questions.question_text: Why does the team run a coordination review before releasing the construction documents?

options.A: Bidders are barred from asking questions after the documents have been released
options.B: The building official requires an overlay of drawings before issuing any permit
options.C: Conflicts between disciplines are cheaper to fix on paper than to discover on site
options.D: Specifications can be replaced by drawings once all sheets have been compared

questions.explanation: Gaps and conflicts do not disappear; they turn up during construction as questions, delays, or change orders. In the duct and beam example, a clash cost a revised sheet on paper but would have stopped the framers on site. The review is a professional practice, not a permit rule, and specifications remain part of the project manual.

questions.question_text: Which term describes products such as switchgear, elevators, or custom windows that take months to manufacture and can control the schedule?

options.A: Long-lead items
options.B: Alternates
options.C: Addenda
options.D: Punch-list items

questions.explanation: Procurement includes ordering long-lead items early so their delivery does not delay construction. Alternates are priced options the owner may add or subtract from the base bid, addenda are written changes to the documents during bidding, and punch-list items are minor corrections at closeout. Only long-lead items are defined by their long manufacturing time.

questions.question_text: A contract is for $2,000,000 with 10 percent retainage. The architect certifies that 25 percent of the work is complete, and $300,000 has been paid previously. What is the payment due this month?
questions.explanation: Earned to date is 0.25 × $2,000,000 = $500,000. Retainage is 10 percent of that, or $50,000, so payment due is $500,000 − $50,000 − $300,000 = $150,000. The value of $450,000 forgets to subtract earlier payments, $200,000 forgets retainage, and $50,000 is only the retainage itself.

questions.question_text: In design-bid-build, when does the builder join the project?

options.A: At the start of design, as an adviser to the architect
options.B: During schematic design, under a single contract with the architect
options.C: At the start, as a signer of a multi-party agreement
options.D: After the design is complete and the documents have been bid

questions.explanation: Design-bid-build is strictly sequential: the architect completes the design, the finished documents are bid, and the contract goes to the low bidder. The owner holds separate contracts with the architect and contractor. Joining at the start as an adviser describes construction manager at risk, and the multi-party agreement describes integrated project delivery.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of commissioning?

options.A: To certify that the contractor's pay application is accurate before the monthly payment is released
options.B: To compare the bids received and award the contract to the lowest responsible bidder
options.C: To verify that installed systems perform to the owner's requirements and the design intent
options.D: To record the building as actually built, including changes made during construction

questions.explanation: Commissioning uses functional tests, in which each system is operated through its modes, to show that heating, emergency lighting, and controls work as intended. Certifying payment is a construction administration task, awarding a contract is part of bidding, and recording as-built conditions is the job of record drawings at closeout.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the role of the architect?

options.A: A licensed design professional who leads the design team and is primarily responsible for the design
options.B: A contractor who manages the site, schedules the trades, and decides means and methods
options.C: A building official who reviews drawings and inspects the finished work for compliance with the adopted code
options.D: A specialty firm hired by the general contractor to perform part of the physical work

questions.explanation: Licensing exists because design errors endanger the public, so a state board verifies the architect's education, experience, and examination record. The architect coordinates the engineers' work and usually holds the design contract with the owner. Managing the site belongs to the general contractor, code review to the building official, and trade work to subcontractors.

questions.question_text: Which document gives legal permission to use a building after the building official's final inspections?

options.A: A certificate of substantial completion
options.B: A punch list
options.C: A certificate of occupancy
options.D: A set of record drawings

questions.explanation: The building official issues the certificate of occupancy if the building complies with the code. Substantial completion is certified by the architect when the owner can use the work, the punch list is a list of minor items still to be corrected, and record drawings show the building as actually built. None of those three grants legal permission to occupy.

questions.question_text: Why does the architect observe the construction work but not supervise it?

options.A: The general contractor controls means and methods and answers for all of the work, including others' work
options.B: The architect lacks a license that permits regular observation visits to the site during construction work
options.C: The owner holds the contract for means and methods and delegates them to subcontractors
options.D: The building official supervises construction, so the architect's visits are only advisory

questions.explanation: The documents describe the finished result, not the process of reaching it. The general contractor holds the prime contract and decides how the work is carried out and in what order, plus schedule and site safety. The architect's periodic visits protect the owner by checking consistency with the design, not by directing the work.

questions.question_text: Why can design-build shorten the schedule compared with design-bid-build?

options.A: The owner skips the design phase and instead uses documents from a similar project built elsewhere
options.B: The contractor submits a sealed bid, so the bidding period is eliminated from the project schedule entirely
options.C: The architect works for the owner independently, so approvals happen in a single step
options.D: One entity holds the contract for design and construction, so early work like foundations can start during design

questions.explanation: Under design-build the owner signs a single contract with one entity responsible for both design and construction, so phases overlap. The trade-offs are less independent oversight of the design and a price set earlier, when less is known. Design is still performed, bids are not the mechanism, and the architect is part of the design-build team, not an independent party.

questions.question_text: What does the construction manager at risk agree to deliver?

options.A: The project for the lowest bid submitted by any qualified general contractor
options.B: The project for a guaranteed maximum price, bearing the risk of overruns above it
options.C: The design and the construction under a single multi-party agreement with shared rewards
options.D: The construction administration services that the architect would normally perform

questions.explanation: In CMAR the owner hires a construction manager during design as an adviser, and the same firm then agrees to build for a guaranteed maximum price. The owner keeps separate contracts with the architect and the construction manager. Selection is based on qualifications and fee, not lowest price alone, and the shared-reward multi-party agreement describes integrated project delivery.

questions.question_text: Why does a Minnesota contractor try to finish the foundation and dry-in before hard winter?

options.A: Interior work can proceed in heated, protected space without the cost of cold-weather measures
options.B: Building codes prohibit pouring foundations or framing walls at any time between December and March
options.C: Subcontractors are unavailable in winter, so only exterior work can be scheduled
options.D: Dried-in buildings no longer need inspections before interior finishes are applied

questions.explanation: Sequencing orders activities for physical reasons, to protect completed work, and to allow inspections. In Minnesota, the calendar adds a constraint: a project not dried in before freezing weather faces temporary heat, cold-weather concrete practices, and delays. Winter work is not prohibited by code, trades remain available, and inspections still occur.

questions.question_text: Why should a project team identify a single person with authority to speak for the owner at the outset?

options.A: Only one person may sign the contract documents under public procurement laws
options.B: The building official will communicate only with a single representative
options.C: Slow or reversed owner decisions are a common source of delay and expense
options.D: The architect cannot hold a design contract with more than one person

questions.explanation: The owner commissions and pays for the project and approves each phase gate. When several people give conflicting answers or reverse decisions, the team loses time and money. Public procurement laws, official communication channels, and architect contracts do not require a single representative, though identifying one is a practical safeguard.

questions.question_text: Why do payments and questions from a subcontractor flow through the general contractor?

options.A: The subcontractor is not licensed to communicate with the architect or engineers
options.B: The subcontractor is paid by the building official after each inspection
options.C: The subcontractor works only on public projects, where direct contact is prohibited
options.D: The subcontractor has a contract with the general contractor and none with the owner

questions.explanation: A subcontractor is a specialty firm hired by the general contractor for a portion of the work, so its contractual relationship runs up to the GC, who remains responsible for the entire chain, including any sub-tier firms. Questions and payments therefore follow that contract path. The reasons given in the other statements are not part of how projects are organized.

questions.question_text: Which feature of integrated project delivery makes it extend construction manager at risk?

options.A: The builder adds cost advice during design but still holds a separate contract directly with the owner
options.B: Designers and builders sign one multi-party agreement and share risk and reward instead of separate contracts
options.C: The owner awards a single lump sum to the lowest bidder after the design is complete and permitted
options.D: The contractor guarantees a maximum price and absorbs any overrun by itself

questions.explanation: IPD brings the owner, architect, contractor, and key subcontractors under one agreement with shared incentives, so decisions move earlier, when change is cheapest. CMAR brings the builder into design but keeps separate contracts and puts the overrun risk on the construction manager. Lowest-bid lump sums describe design-bid-build, and bearing overruns alone describes the GMP in CMAR.

questions.question_text: An electrical subcontractor wants to order a main switchboard. What should happen before the switchboard is ordered?

options.A: The subcontractor orders the switchboard and sends the invoice to the architect for approval
options.B: The subcontractor prepares a submittal, the general contractor checks it, and the engineer reviews it
options.C: The subcontractor sends a request for information asking the owner to approve the manufacturer's switchboard
options.D: The subcontractor asks the building official to approve the switchboard before purchase

questions.explanation: Submittals such as product data and dimensions let the design team confirm that the product meets the specification before it is ordered. The sub prepares it, the GC checks it, and the engineer returns it with a status such as approved or revise and resubmit. An RFI asks a question, not for product approval, and the building official reviews code compliance, not product selection.

questions.question_text: Why do requests for information protect both the contractor and the design team?

options.A: They automatically change the contract price when the design team replies
options.B: They allow the contractor to start extra work without waiting for a signed change order from the owner
options.C: They create a written record of the question, the date, and the answer for any later dispute
options.D: They transfer responsibility for the question to the building official

questions.explanation: An RFI is a written question that clarifies unclear, incomplete, or conflicting documents, and the written answer may become a change to the documents. Because the exchange is on file, both sides can show what was intended. An RFI does not by itself adjust price or authorize extra work; that requires a change order or written directive.

questions.question_text: A superintendent is told verbally at the site to add a small extra wall, and the schedule is tight. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Wait for a signed change order or written directive stating price and time
options.B: Begin the work and settle the price after the extra wall is built
options.C: Build the wall and submit it as a punch-list item at closeout
options.D: Ask the building official to approve the extra wall as a field change before any work starts

questions.explanation: A change order is a written modification of scope, price, or time signed by the owner, architect, and contractor. Starting extra work on a verbal go-ahead leaves price unagreed, so a dispute can leave the contractor unpaid. Punch-list items are minor corrections to contract work, and the building official reviews code compliance, not contract changes.

questions.question_text: Activity A takes 3 days. Activities B (4 days) and C (6 days) both follow A. Activity D takes 2 days and follows both B and C. How many days is the shortest possible project duration?

options.A: 9 days
options.B: 13 days
options.C: 15 days
options.D: 11 days

questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities. A-B-D totals 9 days and A-C-D totals 11 days, so the critical path is A-C-D and the project takes 11 days, with B holding 2 days of float. Choosing 9 follows the shorter chain, 13 adds A, B, and C, and 15 adds every duration as though no activities could overlap.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: A brace carries a 2,000 lb force acting at 30 degrees from the horizontal. What is the vertical component of that force?
questions.explanation: The vertical component is F sin θ = 2,000 × sin 30° = 1,000 lb. The value 1,732 lb is the horizontal component (F cos θ), 2,000 lb treats the whole force as vertical, and 2,732 lb adds the two components as if they were collinear. Components always combine as the sides of a right triangle, not as a simple sum.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: How does heat differ from temperature?

options.A: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, while temperature is average molecular motion
options.B: Heat is the average motion of molecules in a material, while temperature is the energy transferred between objects
options.C: Heat is measured in degrees, while temperature is measured in BTU or joules
options.D: Heat and temperature are the same quantity expressed in different unit systems

questions.explanation: A bathtub of lukewarm water contains much more heat than a sparkler's spark, though the spark is far hotter. Temperature describes how fast molecules move on average, whereas heat is energy in transit between objects at different temperatures. Heat is measured in BTU or joules, temperature in degrees, so the two cannot be interchanged.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Why is it more accurate to say a heated building loses heat in winter than to say cold enters the building?

options.A: Cold is a form of energy that moves from outdoors into the walls, but only through windows and doors
options.B: Heat always flows from warmer to colder regions, so heat leaves through walls, roof, windows, and floor
options.C: Heat flows toward the region with more air, so the warm interior draws in the colder outdoor air
options.D: Heat flows only through conduction, so cold cannot cross the enclosure by other means

questions.explanation: Heat transfer is the movement of heat from higher to lower temperature, and the rate increases with the temperature difference. A draft is warm air leaving and replacement air arriving that the furnace must heat. Cold is not a thing that moves, and heat moves by conduction, convection, and radiation, not conduction alone.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: A 20 ft beam rests on supports A and B at its ends. A 4,000 lb point load sits 5 ft from A. What is the reaction at A?
questions.explanation: Take moments about B: R_A × 20 = 4,000 × 15, so R_A = 3,000 lb. The reaction at B is 1,000 lb, and the two reactions sum to the 4,000 lb load. The support nearer the load carries more of it. Choosing 2,000 lb assumes the load is centered, and 4,000 lb assigns the whole load to one support.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Why does a footing under a post reduce the risk of overloading the soil?

options.A: It reduces the weight of the post so less force reaches the soil
options.B: It spreads the same force over a larger area, so the stress on the soil is lower
options.C: It converts compressive stress in the post into tensile stress in the soil
options.D: It increases the strain in the soil so the soil carries more total force

questions.explanation: Stress equals force divided by area. A 6,000 lb post load on a 2 ft by 2 ft footing is 1,500 psf, far lower than the stress on the post itself. Materials fail when stress at a location reaches their limit, so enlarging the area keeps the soil below its allowable pressure. The footing does not change the load or convert stress types.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Through which materials is conduction the main mechanism of heat transfer?

options.A: Moving fluids such as warm air rising from a radiator or water circulating in a pipe
options.B: Empty space between the sun and a window surface
options.C: Solid building materials such as wood, concrete, steel, and insulation
options.D: Open air gaps and cavities where warm and cool air circulate freely by buoyancy

questions.explanation: Conduction passes heat by collisions between neighboring molecules without bulk motion of the material, so it dominates in solids. Moving fluids transfer heat by convection, and empty space carries heat by radiation. Air gaps involve convection and radiation. Insulation works because trapped still air limits conduction through a mostly gas-filled material.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: A wall has several layers in series between the warm room and the cold outdoors. How do their thermal resistances combine?

options.A: They average, and the temperature drop divides equally among the layers
options.B: They multiply, and the thinnest layer takes the largest share of the temperature drop
options.C: They add, and the layer with the lowest resistance takes the largest share of the temperature drop across the wall
options.D: They add, and the layer with the highest resistance takes the largest share of the temperature drop

questions.explanation: Thermal resistance follows Ohm's law in a thermal costume: layers in series add, like resistors in series. The temperature difference divides in proportion to each layer's resistance, so in the example about 67 of the 80°F drop falls across the insulation. Averaging or multiplying resistances misrepresents series heat flow, and the low-resistance layers take the smallest share.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: A designer needs R-20 of roof insulation. How thick must the layer be if polyisocyanurate board provides R-5 per inch?

options.A: 4 in
options.C: 15 in
options.D: 100 in

questions.explanation: The thickness equals the target R divided by the R per inch: 20 / 5 = 4 in. The value 0.25 in inverts the ratio, 15 in subtracts instead of dividing, and 100 in multiplies. A higher R-value means more resistance, so reaching the target with a material that has more R per inch needs a thinner layer, which matters when the roof is shallow.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Why does a person standing near a large window on a winter day feel chilled even when the thermostat reads 70°F?

options.A: Cold air flows through the glass by conduction and replaces the warm air near the skin and face
options.B: The skin radiates heat toward the colder window surface, and that net radiant loss feels like a chill
options.C: The window emits cold radiation that is absorbed by the skin
options.D: The thermostat is measuring convection, which is unrelated to how warm a surface feels

questions.explanation: Every object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation, and a colder surface returns less than it receives. The worked example shows net exchange to a 40°F pane is about double that to a 68°F wall. Cold is not emitted, and the sensation does not depend on air temperature alone, which is why low-emissivity coatings and warmer inner glass surfaces improve comfort.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes strain?

options.A: It is the internal force divided by the cross-sectional area, in psi
options.B: It is the permanent deformation that remains after any stress is applied
options.C: It is the change in length divided by the original length, and it has no units
options.D: It is the force applied to a member divided by the change in its length

questions.explanation: Strain is ε = ΔL / L, a dimensionless ratio because the two lengths cancel, so 0.001 means one thousandth of the length. The force-over-area quantity is stress, not strain. Permanent deformation describes plastic behavior after the elastic limit is exceeded, and strain by itself says nothing about force divided by deflection.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: A batt labeled R-13 sits between wood studs, yet the framed wall performs well below R-13. What best explains the gap?

options.A: Insulation loses its R-value whenever it touches a stud, so the cavity is effectively uninsulated
options.B: Studs add resistance in parallel, so the total resistance is the sum of the stud and cavity paths
options.C: The R-value on the label includes only the siding and sheathing, not the insulation
options.D: Studs conduct heat more easily than insulation and bypass the cavity, so the effective R is lower

questions.explanation: Heat chooses the easiest path. Studs make up roughly a quarter of a wall's area, and the stud path totals about R-6.8 versus R-15.4 at the cavity, so the area-weighted U-value gives an effective R near 11.7. The label describes the insulation alone, and parallel paths are combined by averaging U-values, not by adding resistances.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: What distinguishes forced convection from natural convection?

options.A: In forced convection a fan, pump, or wind drives the fluid, while in natural convection density drives it
options.B: In forced convection heat travels through solids, while in natural convection it travels through gases
options.C: In forced convection the fluid is still, while in natural convection it moves in layers
options.D: In forced convection electromagnetic waves carry the heat, while in natural convection molecules collide

questions.explanation: Convection is heat transfer by the motion of a fluid. In natural convection, warm fluid is lighter and rises while cool fluid sinks; in forced convection an external agent such as a fan, pump, or wind drives the motion. Heat through solids is conduction and heat by electromagnetic waves is radiation. A moving fluid exchanges heat faster than still air.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: How is the U-value of an assembly related to its R-value?

options.A: It equals the total R-value multiplied by the area
options.B: It equals the reciprocal of the assembly's total R-value
options.C: It equals the sum of the R-values of each layer
options.D: It equals the R-value divided by the temperature difference

questions.explanation: The U-value is the rate of heat flow per square foot per degree, so U = 1 / R_total, with the total including every layer and the air films. Heat loss then equals U × area × ΔT. Summing layer R-values gives the total R, not U, and multiplying by area or dividing by ΔT does not produce the reciprocal.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Why does a fixed overhang on a south window block summer heat but admit winter sun in Minneapolis?

options.A: The noon sun is much higher in summer than in winter, so the overhang shades more glass in summer
options.B: The overhang moves with the seasons so that it covers the window only when the sun is highest
options.C: The summer sun shines from the north side, so the south window needs shading in winter
options.D: The overhang reflects infrared radiation in summer and transmits it in winter

questions.explanation: At about 45° north latitude the noon sun altitude is roughly 68° in June and 22° in December. A 2 ft overhang shades about 81 percent of a 5 ft window in summer but leaves it fully in sun in winter. The overhang is fixed with no moving parts and does not filter radiation by season, and the sun does not shine from the north in summer at noon.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Which property best describes thermal mass?

options.A: A material's resistance to heat flow, determined by its thickness divided by its conductivity
options.B: A material's ability to emit radiation, determined by its emissivity from zero to one
options.C: A material's weight per cubic foot, determined by the load it places on the foundation
options.D: A material's capacity to store heat and release it slowly, determined by its mass and specific heat

questions.explanation: Heavy materials with high specific heat, such as water, concrete, and masonry, absorb much heat per degree and so warm and cool slowly. Resistance to heat flow is thermal resistance, and emissivity describes radiation. Thermal mass delays heat flow but does not stop it, so it cannot substitute for insulation.

questions.chapter: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
questions.question_text: Which rating describes a wall or floor's resistance to airborne sound?

options.A: Impact Insulation Class (IIC)
options.B: Decibel Absorption Rating (DAR)
options.C: Sound Transmission Class (STC)
options.D: Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC)

questions.explanation: Airborne sound such as speech is rated by the Sound Transmission Class, and codes commonly require about STC 50 between dwelling units. The Impact Insulation Class rates resistance to impact sound such as footsteps. Higher numbers are better for both. The other two options are not the building-science ratings for airborne sound through separating walls and floors in this chapter.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Why do designers separate the four ways that moisture reaches a building instead of treating moisture as a single problem?

options.A: Each mechanism affects a different building material, so a single control can be chosen for each material in turn
options.B: Each mechanism occurs in a different season, so controls can be scheduled for the time of year
options.C: Each mechanism has a different driver and needs a different control, so controlling only one leaves the others
options.D: Each mechanism produces the same damage, so any single control protects the whole assembly

questions.explanation: Bulk water is stopped by flashing and drainage, capillary action by breaks in the material, air-carried vapor by an air barrier, and diffusion is slowed by vapor-resistant layers. The mechanisms are separated because their drivers differ, not because of materials or seasons, and a designer who controls only one has left three pathways open.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: A kitchen exhaust hood removes 1,000 CFM from a building that has no makeup air and a gas water heater. Why is this a safety problem as well as a comfort problem?

options.A: The building is pressurized, so warm humid indoor air is pushed into the walls and condenses on the sheathing
options.B: The hood raises the temperature of the kitchen, which lowers the stack pressure that keeps flue gases rising
options.C: The hood reduces wind pressure on the windward wall, which stops the flue from drawing properly
options.D: The building is depressurized, so air is pulled in through every gap, including the flue, carrying gases inside

questions.explanation: Air moves from higher pressure to lower pressure. An exhaust fan that removes more air than enters lowers the indoor pressure, and replacement air comes through every available path, including a water heater flue. Pressurizing describes supply fans, not exhaust fans, and the hood does not change wind pressure on walls.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: A room leaks 40 CFM of outdoor air on a design day when the indoor-outdoor temperature difference is 70°F. Using Q = 1.08 × CFM × ΔT, how much heat must the system supply to warm that air?

options.A: 2,800 BTU/h
options.B: 3,024 BTU/h
options.C: 30 BTU/h
options.D: 4,536 BTU/h

questions.explanation: Substituting into the sensible-heat form for air gives 1.08 × 40 × 70 = 3,024 BTU/h. The result 2,800 BTU/h forgets the 1.08 factor, which combines the density and specific heat of air. The value 30 BTU/h divides instead of multiplies, and 4,536 BTU/h uses a temperature difference of about 105°F. Leakage is a large heat loss that insulation alone does not address.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Why can warm air hold far more water vapor than cold air?

options.A: The saturation limit rises quickly with temperature, so cold air saturates with much less vapor
options.B: The humidity ratio of air is fixed, so warm air only appears to hold more vapor than cold air does
options.C: Cold air condenses its vapor into the walls before it can be measured
options.D: Warm air is denser than cold air, so it displaces more vapor in each cubic foot of space

questions.explanation: Air holds a maximum amount of vapor at a given temperature, and that saturation limit rises quickly with warming. At 70°F saturated air holds about 27 times as much vapor as saturated air at −10°F. The humidity ratio is not fixed, and warm air is lighter than cold air, not denser, so density does not explain the difference.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: A sealed parcel of air at 40 percent RH is warmed by 20°F with no water added. Using the rule of twenty, what is the RH afterward?

options.A: About 40 percent
options.B: About 20 percent
options.C: About 80 percent
options.D: About 100 percent

questions.explanation: The saturation limit roughly doubles for every 20°F of warming, so the same amount of vapor represents about half the capacity and the RH falls to about 20 percent. RH stays at 40 only if temperature is unchanged. The values 80 and 100 reverse the rule, which applies to cooling, where RH roughly doubles until the air reaches saturation.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: How does the dew point differ from relative humidity?

options.A: The dew point does not change when air is warmed or cooled, only when moisture is added or removed
options.B: The dew point rises when air is warmed, while relative humidity stays constant as the air heats
options.C: The dew point is the temperature at which relative humidity becomes zero percent
options.D: The dew point changes with the temperature of the surrounding surfaces but not with vapor content

questions.explanation: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, with no change in vapor content, for it to become saturated. Because it measures the vapor itself, it is stable under heating or cooling, whereas RH changes with temperature. A higher dew point means more moisture in the air, and surface temperatures do not alter the air's dew point.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Why can vapor diffusion occur through gypsum board even when the air is perfectly still?

options.A: Vapor is carried through the board by pressure differences that push moving air across the whole wall
options.B: Vapor condenses on the warm face of the board and is drawn through by capillary action
options.C: Vapor passes only through Class I vapor retarders, which are driven by temperature differences between faces
options.D: Vapor molecules migrate through tiny pores from the side of higher vapor pressure to the side of lower pressure

questions.explanation: Diffusion is driven by a difference in vapor pressure, not by moving air. In winter the heated interior holds more vapor than the cold outdoors, so vapor pushes outward through porous materials. It usually moves far less water than air leakage does, and retarders slow it rather than being the only path.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Which building would experience the strongest stack-driven pressure difference?

options.A: A short building on a mild day, because the neutral pressure plane then sits near the roof
options.B: A tall building on a mild day, because warm air rises faster in taller shafts
options.C: A tall building on a very cold day, because the effect grows with height and temperature difference
options.D: A short building on a very cold day, because cold air is denser near the ground floor

questions.explanation: The stack effect arises from differences in air density between warm interior and cold exterior air. Stack pressure is about proportional to height times the difference of the reciprocals of absolute temperatures, so it increases with both height and temperature difference. That is why stairwells and elevator shafts in tall cold-climate buildings produce noticeable drafts.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Groundwater is wicking from a concrete footing into a wood sill plate above it. Which detail best stops this?

options.A: A thicker coat of paint on the exposed face of the sill plate and the adjacent wall
options.B: A membrane between the footing and the sill that breaks the continuous pore path
options.C: A tighter air barrier installed on the interior side of the exterior wall
options.D: A vapor retarder installed below the finished floor of the room above

questions.explanation: Capillary action draws liquid water through narrow pores by surface tension, and concrete, masonry, and brick are full of such pores. A capillary break such as a membrane, coarse gravel, or damp-proofing interrupts the continuous path, because water cannot climb across a large gap. Paint, air barriers, and vapor retarders do not address liquid water wicking.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Why can a well-insulated building with warm interior surfaces feel comfortable at a lower air temperature?

options.A: Air speed is the only factor of comfort, so warm surfaces reduce the speed of drafts near the windows
options.B: Comfort depends only on humidity, so insulation raises the humidity near the surfaces of the room
options.C: Warm surfaces raise the thermostat reading, so occupants perceive the room as warmer
options.D: Mean radiant temperature is a factor of comfort, so warm surfaces reduce radiant heat loss from occupants

questions.explanation: Comfort depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, metabolic rate, and clothing insulation. A person near a cold window loses heat by radiation and feels chilled at 70°F, while warm surfaces reduce that loss. The thermostat measures air temperature alone and is not changed by surface warmth.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: On a psychrometric chart, how do you find the dew point of air at a given state point?

options.A: Move horizontally to the left at constant humidity ratio until you reach the saturation curve
options.B: Move vertically upward at constant temperature until you reach the saturation curve
options.C: Move horizontally to the right at constant humidity ratio until you reach the saturation curve
options.D: Move along the constant relative humidity line until it meets the dry-bulb axis

questions.explanation: The horizontal axis is dry-bulb temperature and the vertical axis is humidity ratio. Sliding left keeps the vapor content unchanged while the air cools, and the temperature where the path meets the 100 percent saturation curve is the dew point. Moving right is heating, and moving vertically changes the vapor content, which defeats the definition.

questions.chapter: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
questions.question_text: Why is concealed condensation more dangerous than visible condensation on a window?

options.A: It occurs only in winter, when freezing prevents materials from drying afterward in the spring
options.B: It releases latent heat as the vapor condenses, which damages the surrounding materials directly
options.C: It occurs inside walls, attics, and roofs, where it can wet insulation and framing for months unnoticed
options.D: It forms only on the warm side of the wall, where the structural members are located inside

questions.explanation: Condensation happens when humid air touches a surface at or below its dew point. Visible condensation on glass or pipes is noticed and wiped away, while concealed condensation can wet insulation, framing, and sheathing for months. It occurs on the cold side of the wall in winter, and in summer cold ducts and pipes can sweat, so it is not limited to one season.

questions.question_text: Why is the load a particular steel rod can carry a property of the member rather than of the material?

options.A: It depends on the rod's cross-sectional area, while a material property does not depend on size or shape
options.B: It depends on the temperature of the steel, while a material property is measured at a fixed temperature
options.C: It depends on how the steel was manufactured, while a material property is identical for all steels
options.D: It depends on the standard used to test the steel, while a material property is untested

questions.explanation: A material property, such as yield stress, belongs to the material and is the same for a rod or a beam. Capacity equals the property multiplied by the size you chose, using the stress, force, and area relationships from Chapter 3. This distinction lets designers compare materials fairly and then convert the property into the capacity of an actual member.

questions.question_text: A steel hanger rod has a yield strength of 36,000 psi and carries a working stress of 18,000 psi. What is its factor of safety against yielding?
questions.explanation: The factor of safety is the ratio of strength to working stress: 36,000 / 18,000 = 2.0. The value 0.5 inverts the ratio, which would mean the rod had already yielded. Designers never load a member to its strength, and apply a factor of safety to allow for unknown loads, variations in material, and workmanship.

questions.question_text: A 10 in by 10 in concrete column carries 80,000 lb. What is the working compressive stress?

options.B: 80 psi
options.C: 800 psi

questions.explanation: Stress equals force divided by area. The area is 10 × 10 = 100 in², so the stress is 80,000 / 100 = 800 psi, about 20 percent of a typical 4,000 psi concrete strength. The value 8,000 psi divides by 10 in², 80 psi divides by 1,000 in², and 4,000 psi is the specified compressive strength, not the working stress.

questions.question_text: A concrete sidewalk without air entrainment is cracked and flaking after several Minnesota winters. What best explains the damage?

options.A: Ultraviolet light broke down the cement, which reduced the compressive strength of the slab
options.B: Water in the pores froze and expanded about 9 percent, and the ice had no room to expand
options.C: Thermal contraction pulled the slab apart because concrete has a very high coefficient of expansion
options.D: Corrosion of the sidewalk's steel reinforcement pushed the surface off the slab

questions.explanation: Freeze-thaw cycling is often the most damaging weathering process in Minnesota. When pores are more than about 92 percent full, expanding ice cracks the surface, especially on horizontal surfaces that stay wet. Air entrainment, with 5 to 7 percent microscopic bubbles, gives the freezing water room to expand. UV light mainly harms plastics, paints, and sealants.

questions.question_text: Why is fire resistance expressed as a rating in hours for an assembly rather than as a property of a bare material?

options.A: It is measured by exposing a full-scale element to a standard fire and checking that it keeps performing
options.B: It is calculated from the density of the material and the thickness of the layer being tested in the furnace
options.C: It is the time a material takes to ignite, so it applies to the individual material only
options.D: It is determined by flame spread tests, which compare the surface of one material with another

questions.explanation: Fire resistance is the ability of a wall, floor, or beam to keep performing its function for a stated period, determined by the ASTM E119 standard fire test. The element must carry load, resist flame passage, and limit heat rise on the unexposed face. Ignition and flame spread describe combustibility, which belongs to the material, not the assembly.

questions.question_text: Why is rebar placed near the bottom face of a simply supported concrete beam loaded from above?

options.A: The bottom is squeezed when the beam bends, and concrete is weakest in compression, so rebar is placed there
options.B: The bottom is stretched when the beam bends, and concrete's tensile strength is only about a tenth of its compressive
options.C: The bottom carries the greatest shear force, and rebar prevents the beam from splitting along its grain
options.D: The bottom is exposed to moisture, and rebar protects it from freeze-thaw damage

questions.explanation: A loaded beam bends: the top is squeezed and the bottom is stretched. Concrete handles the compression but cracks in tension, so steel bars placed where the tension is pick up the stretching force. A single #5 bar carries about 18,600 lb in tension. Concrete is strong in compression, and rebar's role here is carrying tension, not preventing freeze-thaw damage.

questions.question_text: A 50 ft steel member (coefficient 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °F) experiences a 100°F temperature swing. By about how much does its length change?

options.B: 3.9 in

questions.explanation: Using ΔL = α L ΔT with L = 600 in gives 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 600 × 100 = 0.39 in. Using 50 instead of 600 in forgets the unit conversion, 0.039 in is a decimal slip, 3.9 in is ten times too large, and 0.78 in doubles the length. Long buildings need expansion joints for this reason.

questions.question_text: Why are concrete test cylinders cast from the same batch and cured under controlled conditions?

options.A: The cylinders are used to measure the porosity of the concrete in the structure rather than its strength
options.B: The cylinders are cast first so that the building's concrete can be poured at a later date
options.C: The concrete cannot be tested before it is placed, so cylinders represent it at the standard 28-day age
options.D: The cylinders replace the need for any field tests such as slump or air content

questions.explanation: Because concrete is poured on site and cannot be tested before placement, cylinders from the same batch stand in for it. They are loaded in a press at 28 days to find the compressive strength, for example 113,100 lb on 28.3 in² gives 4,000 psi. Field tests such as slump and air content still occur on each delivery.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes stiffness from strength?

options.A: Stiffness is resistance to deformation under load, while strength is the stress at which a material fails or yields
options.B: Stiffness is the stress at which a material fails, while strength is resistance to deformation under load
options.C: Stiffness and strength are the same property, measured in psi for stiff and strong materials alike
options.D: Stiffness describes how much energy a material absorbs before fracture, while strength describes how it bends

questions.explanation: A stiff material changes shape little under load, and a strong material resists higher stress before failing. A steel spring is strong and flexible, glass is stiff and brittle, and a floor can be strong enough yet feel bouncy. Energy absorbed before fracture is toughness, so check both stress and deflection in design.

questions.question_text: What does ductility describe?

options.A: The ability of a material to absorb impact energy at low temperatures without cracking
options.B: The ability of a material to deform plastically by a large amount before it fractures
options.C: The tendency of a material to fracture suddenly with little or no plastic deformation first
options.D: The slow continuing deformation of a material under a sustained load

questions.explanation: A ductile material such as A36 steel can stretch about 20 percent before breaking, so it sags or bends visibly and gives warning of overload. The tendency to fracture suddenly is brittleness, absorbed energy is toughness, and slow continuing deformation under sustained load is creep.

questions.question_text: How do creep and shrinkage differ from the instant elastic strain described in Chapter 3?

options.A: Both are permanent deformations that occur only after a material has exceeded its yield strength
options.B: Both are reversible deformations that disappear as soon as the load or moisture is removed
options.C: Both are caused by thermal expansion, which is why they occur in Minnesota's wide temperature swings
options.D: Both are changes over time, with creep under sustained load and shrinkage as a material loses moisture

questions.explanation: Elastic strain appears immediately when a load is applied. Creep is slow, continuing deformation under sustained load, and shrinkage is the volume reduction as moisture leaves. Wood floor beams deflect more after a few years, and concrete shrinks by about 500 microstrain, which is why control joints are cut in slabs. Neither requires yielding, and neither is a temperature effect.

questions.question_text: Which description best defines porosity?

options.A: The ease with which a fluid passes through a material, measured in perms or similar units
options.B: The stress at which a material begins to deform permanently under a sustained tensile load
options.C: The fraction of a material's volume that is empty space, expressed as a percentage
options.D: The ratio of a material's weight to its volume, measured in pounds per cubic foot

questions.explanation: Porosity measures empty volume, such as the voids in brick, concrete, wood, and stone. It underlies capillary wicking and freeze-thaw damage, and high porosity lowers density and strength but improves insulating value. The ease of fluid passage is permeability, the stress threshold is yield strength, and weight per volume is density.

questions.question_text: A specification cites "ASTM A36" for structural members. Using the first-letter convention, what subject does this standard cover?

options.A: Concrete and masonry products
options.B: Nonferrous metals such as aluminum
options.C: Fire tests and miscellaneous subjects
options.D: Ferrous metals such as structural steel

questions.explanation: The first letter of an ASTM designation indicates the subject: A is ferrous metals like steel, B is nonferrous metals, C is concrete and masonry, D is miscellaneous materials such as wood and plastics, and E is miscellaneous subjects including fire tests. A36 specifies a grade of structural steel. A standard is voluntary until a code or contract requires it, and then it becomes binding.

questions.question_text: Which type of element is governed mainly by shear strength?

options.A: Hanger rods and cables that hang loads from above
options.B: Columns and footings carrying weight to the ground
options.C: Bolts, welds, nails, and beam connections
options.D: Concrete cylinders crushed in a test press

questions.explanation: Shear strength is the maximum shear stress a material can withstand before one part slides past another. It governs connections, and in wood it also matters at beam ends, where a board can split lengthwise. Hanger rods and cables are governed by tensile strength, and columns, footings, and crushed cylinders are governed by compressive strength.

questions.question_text: Steel with a modulus of elasticity of 29,000,000 psi carries an elastic stress of 14,500 psi. What is its strain?
questions.explanation: The modulus equals stress divided by strain, so strain equals stress divided by modulus: 14,500 / 29,000,000 = 0.0005, or 500 microstrain. The values 0.005 and 0.00005 are decimal slips, and 2,000 comes from dividing the modulus by the stress. Strain is dimensionless, so it should be a small number rather than a large one.

questions.question_text: Why is it a mistake to treat a brittle material as a weak one?

options.A: Glass is strong in compression yet breaks without warning, so brittleness describes how failure occurs, not strength
options.B: Brittle materials always have a high yield strength, so they fail only under very large and sustained loads on them
options.C: Brittle materials deform plastically by large amounts, so they are generally stronger than ductile ones in tension
options.D: Brittleness is determined only by temperature, so one material can be brittle in winter and strong in summer

questions.explanation: Brittleness is the tendency to fracture with little or no plastic deformation, often suddenly. Glass, cast iron, unreinforced concrete, and most masonry are brittle, yet they can be strong in compression. Designers use brittle materials where they are mostly compressed and add reinforcing steel to concrete. A brittle failure gives no warning, so it requires bigger margins.

questions.question_text: Why is steel tough but glass is not, even though both are stiff?

options.A: Steel has a lower modulus of elasticity than glass, so it absorbs impacts by bending elastically without cracking
options.B: Steel is noncombustible while glass can burn, so steel absorbs more energy in a fire than the glass does
options.C: Steel is less dense than glass, so impacts transfer less energy through it into the surrounding frame
options.D: Steel combines strength with ductility, so it absorbs much energy before fracturing, shown by a large curve area

questions.explanation: Toughness is the energy absorbed before fracture, represented by the area under the stress-strain curve. Steel's strength and ductility give a large area, while brittle glass fractures with little energy absorbed. Toughness depends on temperature, so some steels become more brittle in extreme cold and cold-climate specifications may require minimum impact toughness.

questions.question_text: A concrete slab 6 in thick weighs 150 lb/ft³. What is the weight of the slab per square foot of floor area?

options.A: 900 psf
options.B: 25 psf
options.C: 75 psf
options.D: 150 psf

questions.explanation: Multiplying density by thickness gives the weight per square foot of a layer: 150 × (6/12) = 75 psf. The value 900 psf multiplies by 6 without converting inches to feet, 25 psf divides by 6, and 150 psf is the unit weight of the concrete, not the weight of a 6 in layer. This dead load must be carried before anything else.

questions.question_text: A closed-cell foam is highly porous yet nearly impermeable to water vapor. What explains this?

options.A: Its voids are too large to hold water, so any vapor that enters flows straight through
options.B: Its voids are sealed off from one another, and permeability requires the pores to be connected
options.C: Its pores are connected but filled with air, so vapor cannot enter without capillary action
options.D: Its permeance is measured in perms, so the foam's high porosity is not counted

questions.explanation: Permeability is the ease with which a fluid passes through a material. Porosity measures empty volume, but fluid passes through only if the pores are connected to one another. Sealed cells block passage, which is why closed-cell foam can be a very effective vapor-resistant layer, whereas gypsum board is moderate and some house wraps are highly permeable.

questions.question_text: Why can an unprotected steel beam be less reliable in a fire than a large timber beam, even though steel is noncombustible?

options.A: Fire resistance depends on performance, not just burning: steel loses half its strength near 1,100°F
options.B: Steel is combustible in thick sections, while timber becomes noncombustible once it has dried to equilibrium
options.C: Fire resistance is measured only for combustible materials, so unprotected steel cannot be rated at all
options.D: Timber has a higher flame spread index than steel, so it acts as a better barrier to flames in a fire

questions.explanation: Combustibility is a material property tested by ASTM E136, while fire resistance is an assembly's ability to keep performing. Steel can reach about 1,100°F within minutes in the standard fire, and it loses about half its strength, so it is usually covered. A large timber chars at about 1.5 in per hour, and the char insulates the wood beneath it.

questions.question_text: A contractor fastens aluminum flashing with steel screws on a damp exterior wall. Which concern does this raise?

options.A: Thermal creep, in which the two metals move at different rates and gradually loosen the screws
options.B: Brittle failure, in which steel screws fracture without warning when they contact aluminum flashing
options.C: Permeability loss, in which the aluminum prevents vapor from leaving the wall assembly
