options.D: Galvanic corrosion, in which the more reactive metal corrodes faster when two metals touch in moisture

questions.explanation: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two different metals are in contact in the presence of moisture, and the more reactive one corrodes faster. Mixing aluminum and steel fasteners can therefore cause problems. Protection works by keeping oxygen and water from the metal, using paint, galvanizing, stainless steel, or compatible fasteners. The other options describe unrelated behaviors.

questions.question_text: What is the usual order of steps in material selection?

options.A: Compare the costs of all candidates, choose the cheapest, and then identify the properties it must satisfy in use
options.B: Choose the strongest material, list the requirements it fails, and then replace it with a weaker one that passes
options.C: List the requirements, identify the governing properties, compare candidates and eliminate failures, then weigh the rest
options.D: Test every candidate to failure, rank the results by strength, and select the highest-ranked material overall

questions.explanation: Material selection uses properties as evidence. After eliminating materials that fail a requirement such as load, span, moisture exposure, or fire rating, designers weigh cost, availability, constructability, and environmental impact. The choice is almost always a compromise, as in choosing glued-laminated beams for Riverbend even though steel is stronger for a given size.

questions.question_text: Which three requirements must a structural system satisfy at the same time?

options.A: Strength, durability, and affordability
options.B: Stiffness, ductility, and toughness
options.C: Strength, stiffness, and stability
options.D: Stability, permeability, and fire resistance

questions.explanation: The structural system collects loads and carries them safely to the ground. Members must not break or yield (strength), must deform only a small amount (stiffness), and the whole structure must keep its shape and position without tipping, buckling, or racking (stability). Each fails differently, so a designer checks all three. The other combinations mix in material properties or concerns outside the structural job.

questions.question_text: A building carries its gravity loads perfectly but collapses sideways in a windstorm. Which principle from the chapter best explains this?

options.A: Loads flow toward the more flexible route, so wind loads bypassed the stiff walls entirely
options.B: Gravity loads always travel through the lateral system, which was overloaded by the roof's weight
options.C: A load path is required only for loads that act downward, so wind was not part of the design
options.D: Gravity and lateral loads each need their own complete path, and a path for one does not serve the other

questions.explanation: A load path is the continuous route from the point of application through each member and connection to the soil, and it must exist for every load. The chapter notes that a building may carry its gravity load perfectly yet fail sideways because the lateral path was never designed. Loads flow toward the stiffer route, not the more flexible one.

questions.question_text: Why does the code require 100 psf for an assembly space when a packed crowd weighs only about 29 psf?

options.A: Live load is a design allowance covering furniture, equipment, dynamic motion, and uncertainty about future use
options.B: Live load is calculated from the weight of the structure, so it is always larger than the crowd weight alone
options.C: Live load includes snow and wind, so the code adds those to the weight of the people
options.D: Live load is measured after construction, so the code uses the highest value ever recorded

questions.explanation: The code specifies minimum design live loads by occupancy, chosen to cover realistic worst cases such as crowding, stage equipment, and dancing. The 29 psf figure is only the actual weight of 400 adults on 2,400 ft². Weight of the structure itself is dead load, and snow and wind are separate loads in the code's classification.

questions.question_text: A roof assembly has a membrane at 1.0 psf, rigid insulation at 1.5 psf, sheathing at 2.0 psf, joists at 3.0 psf, and a ceiling with services at 4.5 psf. What is the dead load?

options.A: 10.5 psf
options.B: 12.0 psf
options.C: 13.5 psf
options.D: 4.5 psf

questions.explanation: Dead load is the sum of the permanent weights: 1.0 + 1.5 + 2.0 + 3.0 + 4.5 = 12.0 psf. The value 10.5 omits the 1.5 psf of insulation, 13.5 overcounts, and 4.5 psf is just the ceiling. Dead load is the most predictable load, yet it is the one a designer can least afford to underestimate because every other load is added to it.

questions.question_text: In what order does a gravity load pass through the building, from the roof surface down?

options.A: Deck, columns, joists, girders and beams, bearing walls, then foundation
options.B: Joists, deck, bearing walls, beams and girders, columns, then the foundation
options.C: Foundation, columns and walls, girders and beams, joists, then the roof deck
options.D: Deck, joists, beams and girders, columns and bearing walls, then foundation

questions.explanation: The gravity load system hands loads from many small closely spaced members to fewer, larger members: the deck spreads load to joists, joists pass it to beams or girders, those pass it to columns or bearing walls, and the foundation spreads it into the soil. The pattern repeats in every building, with fewer, larger, more widely spaced members at each step down.

questions.question_text: Why is a 2×8 plank much stiffer when set on edge than when laid flat?

options.A: Stiffness depends on the cube of the depth, so the deeper orientation raises the moment of inertia greatly
options.B: Stiffness depends on the width squared, so the wider face carries load better when it faces upward
options.C: Stiffness depends on the area alone, so the plank gains extra area when it is turned on its edge
options.D: Stiffness depends on the material, and wood is stronger along its edge than across its flat face

questions.explanation: For a rectangular beam I = b d³ / 12, so depth enters as the cube. A 2×8 set on edge has I of about 47.6 in⁴ versus about 2.04 in⁴ when flat, roughly 23 times stiffer. The area is the same in both orientations, and the wood's material properties do not change. A beam is always set on edge for this reason.

questions.question_text: Why does a tall, slender column fail at a lower load than a short, stocky column made of the same material?

options.A: It fails by crushing, because the longer member has more material that reaches its strength
options.B: It fails in tension, because slender members cannot carry compression forces along their length
options.C: It fails by buckling, a sudden sideways bowing, before the material reaches its compressive strength
options.D: It fails by shear, because the supports twist the member at both ends under the applied load

questions.explanation: Slender columns are flexible, like a yardstick pressed at its ends. The Euler buckling load depends on E, the smallest moment of inertia, and the square of the unsupported length. A 4×4 post of 10 ft can buckle at about 12,000 lb, while a 6×6 has about six times the capacity. Short, stocky columns fail by crushing instead.

questions.question_text: Using q ≈ 0.00256 V², by what factor does the velocity pressure change when the wind speed doubles from 60 mph to 120 mph?

options.A: It increases by a factor of 2
options.B: It increases by a factor of 4
options.C: It increases by a factor of 8
options.D: It increases by a factor of 16

questions.explanation: Because speed is squared, doubling it quadruples the pressure: about 9.2 psf at 60 mph and about 36.9 psf at 120 mph. A factor of 2 would apply if pressure were proportional to speed, while 8 and 16 assume a cube or fourth-power relationship, which describes other quantities such as deflection versus span but not wind pressure.

questions.question_text: Why does replacing a light roof with a heavy masonry roof increase the seismic force on a building?

options.A: Base shear depends on the exposed area, so a heavy roof presents more surface to the ground motion
options.B: Base shear is a fraction of the building's weight, so greater mass produces a greater inertial force
options.C: Base shear depends on wind speed, so a heavy roof receives a larger share of the wind force
options.D: Base shear depends on the soil only, so the roof weight changes how the force is resisted

questions.explanation: When the ground shakes, the building's mass resists the motion because of inertia, and the horizontal force is V = C_s W. Doubling the roof weight in the example doubles V from 8.5 to 17 kips, exceeding the wind force. Wind scales with area and speed squared, whereas earthquakes scale with weight, so heavy buildings worry about quakes and light, large ones about wind.

questions.question_text: Why can trusses span long distances using little material?

options.A: Triangles cannot change shape, so each member carries only axial tension or compression
options.B: Trusses are always built from steel, which has a very high strength-to-weight ratio
options.C: Truss members carry bending along their length, which uses the full cross-section
options.D: Trusses spread load over the entire roof, which removes the need for supports

questions.explanation: A truss is a framework of straight members arranged in triangles and loaded at its joints. A pinned four-sided frame can rack, but a triangle cannot change shape unless a member changes length. Members loaded axially use their material efficiently. Trusses can be wood with connector plates or steel, and they still need supports at their ends.

questions.question_text: What are the three links by which the lateral load system carries wind to the foundation?

options.A: Footings resist the wind, columns spread it to the soil, and beams deliver it to the exterior walls
options.B: The roof deck resists the wind, joists collect the force, and girders carry it to the posts
options.C: Walls span vertically, a horizontal diaphragm collects the force, and vertical elements carry it down
options.D: Posts receive the wind, the foundation deflects it, and the soil carries it back up to the walls

questions.explanation: The lateral system supplies resistance that the gravity system lacks. Walls receive pressure and pass it to the roof edge and ground, a diaphragm collects those forces and spreads them to vertical resisting elements, and those elements carry the force down. Without it, a building would be like a cardboard box with unglued flaps, able to carry a book on top but ready to collapse sideways.

questions.question_text: Wind suction is 24 psf, and 60 percent of a 15 psf dead load resists it. A girder end has 200 ft² of tributary roof, and its bracket is rated for 2,500 lb of uplift. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: Adequate, because net uplift of about 1,800 lb is below the 2,500 lb rating
options.B: Adequate, because the full dead load offsets the suction, leaving no uplift
options.C: Inadequate, because the net pressure is 24 psf, which multiplies to 4,800 lb
options.D: Inadequate, because net uplift of about 3,000 lb exceeds the 2,500 lb rating

questions.explanation: Net upward pressure is 24 − 0.6 × 15 = 15 psf, and 15 × 200 = 3,000 lb, so the demand exceeds the 2,500 lb capacity (a ratio of 1.2). Counting only part of the dead load is the code's rule where dead load helps. Using the full suction ignores that offset, and counting no suction misreads the check. Uplift connections are specified by the engineer, not left to the framer.

questions.question_text: A code gives a ground snow load of 40 psf, and the adjustments for a heated flat roof in typical exposure give a factor of about 0.7. What is the roof snow load?

options.A: 40 psf
options.B: 57 psf
options.C: 12 psf
options.D: 28 psf

questions.explanation: The designer adjusts the ground snow load for exposure, heat loss, slope, and importance: 0.7 × 40 = 28 psf. Using 40 psf skips the adjustment, 57 psf divides by 0.7 instead of multiplying, and 12 psf subtracts the factor. Uniform snow is only part of the story, since drifting against parapets and roof steps can create local loads several times higher.

questions.question_text: What does "16 in. o.c." mean when describing joist spacing?

options.A: The joists are spaced 16 in. apart, measured from the center of one joist to the center of the next
options.B: The joists are 16 in. deep, measured from the top of the joist to its bottom edge at the support
options.C: The joists may span a maximum of 16 in. before they must be supported by a beam or girder
options.D: The joists are 16 in. long, measured from the support to the first connection at the beam

questions.explanation: Joists are closely spaced horizontal members that support a floor or roof deck, commonly at 12, 16, or 24 in. on center. Because they are close together and tied by the deck, a heavily loaded joist can share load with neighbors. Blocking or bridging between them keeps tall, thin joists from twisting. On center never refers to depth or span.

questions.question_text: How does a roof diaphragm resist lateral force?

options.A: It acts like a column, with the sheathing resisting buckling and the chords resisting crushing forces
options.B: It acts like a deep beam lying on its side, with chords resisting bending and sheathing resisting shear
options.C: It acts like a truss, with the chords carrying shear and the sheathing carrying bending moments
options.D: It acts like a footing, with the sheathing spreading the force into the soil

questions.explanation: A diaphragm is a large, flat, horizontal element such as a roof deck or floor. It collects wind or seismic force from the walls and delivers it to shear walls or frames. The edges, called chords, resist tension and compression from bending, while the sheathing resists shear. Large openings for skylights or stairs reduce its capacity and need special reinforcement.

questions.question_text: Why does the code not add snow load and roof live load together in a load combination?

options.A: Snow load already contains the roof live load, so adding them would count it twice
options.B: Roof live load applies only to floors, so it does not belong in a roof combination
options.C: Workers and heavy snow are not expected at the same time, so the larger of the two governs
options.D: The code treats both loads as permanent, so only one may be counted in a combination

questions.explanation: Load combinations scale and add loads according to how likely they are to occur together, since a crowded room is unlikely to coincide with the worst storm. Roof live load represents workers and maintenance, so it is not combined with heavy snow, and the larger governs. Neither load is permanent. Where dead load helps, as in resisting uplift, only part of it counts.

questions.question_text: A roof carries 50 psf and interior members are spaced 12 ft apart. What line load does each member carry?

options.A: 600 plf
options.B: 300 plf
options.C: 62 plf
options.D: 4.2 plf

questions.explanation: The tributary width is the spacing between interior members, so w = q × b = 50 × 12 = 600 plf. Using half the spacing gives 300, adding the numbers gives 62, and dividing gives 4.2. The tributary area extends halfway to the next supporting member on each side, which for an interior member is the full spacing between members.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes a girder from an ordinary beam?

options.A: A girder is a beam that carries only its own weight and the finishes on it
options.B: A girder is a vertical member that carries load mainly in compression
options.C: A girder is a diagonal member that triangulates a frame so it cannot rack
options.D: A girder is a primary beam that supports other beams, usually joists

questions.explanation: The glulam members over Riverbend's multipurpose room are girders because they receive concentrated loads from many joists and carry them across the span to posts. A girder generally has a larger tributary width, so it is deeper and heavier than the members it supports. Vertical compression members are columns, and diagonal members that stop racking are braces.

questions.question_text: A homeowner wants to remove an interior wall that looks like a partition. Which observation indicates that the wall is bearing?

options.A: It has door openings of standard height
options.B: It is built from studs at 16 in. on center
options.C: Joists or a beam end rest on top of it
options.D: It carries only its own weight and the finish on it

questions.explanation: Bearing walls carry vertical load from floors or roof above, delivered continuously along their length. If joists, trusses, or a beam end rest on a wall, removing it breaks the load path, so the homeowner should check which way the framing runs and consult a structural engineer. A wall that carries only itself is a non-bearing partition, and openings or stud spacing do not decide the question.

questions.question_text: Why is each end of a wood shear wall anchored to the foundation with hold-downs?

options.A: A wall pushed in its own plane tries to slide, and hold-downs resist the sliding directly
options.B: A wall pushed in its own plane tries to tip over, and hold-downs resist the resulting uplift
options.C: A wall under gravity load tries to buckle, and hold-downs keep the studs straight
options.D: A wall under wind suction tries to crack, and hold-downs spread the cracks along the length

questions.explanation: A shear wall resists lateral forces acting in its own plane by shearing, as a deck of cards slides when pushed from the top. The pushed wall tends to overturn, so steel hold-downs resist uplift at its ends. A longer wall resists more, and large openings reduce capacity. Sliding is resisted mainly by the foundation, and buckling and cracking are not the purpose of hold-downs.

questions.question_text: Why do slender X-braced rod diagonals work in tension only?

options.A: In each direction of push both diagonals are stretched equally, so neither one ever carries any compression
options.B: A rod diagonal carries compression easily, so the second diagonal is only needed for redundancy in the frame
options.C: In each direction of push one diagonal stretches and the other goes slack, since a rod cannot resist compression
options.D: The rods are connected at their center, so they always pull on the corners of the frame together at once

questions.explanation: Bracing triangulates a rectangular frame so it cannot rack, the same principle as a truss. Slender rods can pull but buckle in compression, so in an X pattern the diagonal that would be compressed goes slack while the other works in tension. Braced frames are stiff and efficient but interrupt openings, so architects must locate them with care.

questions.question_text: An architect wants a storefront with no diagonal braces or solid walls in the openings. What trade-off comes with using a moment frame instead of a braced frame?

options.A: The frame is stiffer and needs fewer connections, but its beams must be placed inside walls
options.B: The frame is more flexible and needs larger members and more complex connections
options.C: The frame cannot resist wind, so a separate shear wall must be added to every opening
options.D: The frame resists force only in tension, so slender rods must be added to each joint

questions.explanation: A moment frame has rigid beam-to-column joints that resist rotation, so force is carried through bending rather than diagonals, leaving openings free. In exchange, it is more flexible than a braced frame and needs larger members and more complex connections. Steel and reinforced concrete are the common materials. It does resist wind, and its members carry bending, not just tension.

questions.question_text: By what factor does the deflection of a simply supported beam with a uniform load change when its span is doubled, with all else unchanged?

options.A: It is multiplied by 16
options.B: It is multiplied by 2
options.C: It is multiplied by 4
options.D: It is multiplied by 8

questions.explanation: In δ = 5wL⁴ / 384EI, deflection grows with the fourth power of the span, so doubling it multiplies deflection by 2⁴ = 16. A factor of 2 would apply to a linear relationship, 4 to a squared one, and 8 to a cube, which is how depth enters the moment of inertia. Codes limit deflection to a fraction of span, such as L/360, so floors do not sag or crack finishes.

questions.question_text: A designer calculates the area of a nominal 2×6 stud for a load check. Which area should be used?

options.A: 8.25 in², from the actual size of 1.5 in. by 5.5 in.
options.B: 12.0 in², from the nominal size of 2 in. by 6 in. used in the lumber's name
options.C: 7.0 in², from a size of 1.5 in. by 4.5 in.
options.D: 5.5 in², from the width of the face alone

questions.explanation: Lumber is sold by nominal size, a rounded name, but the actual size is smaller because the piece loses material in drying and planing. Structural calculations always use the actual size, so a 2×6 is 1.5 × 5.5 in. = 8.25 in². Using the nominal 2 × 6 overstates the area by almost half, which makes the member look stronger than it is.

questions.question_text: Why can an I-joist be nearly as stiff as a sawn 2×12 while using about half the wood?

options.A: Its web is made of steel, which supplies most of the stiffness without adding any wood to the joist
options.B: Its flanges are cross-laminated, so the grain of each layer resists bending in both directions
options.C: Its adhesive bonds expand when loaded, which raises the moment of inertia of the thin web
options.D: Its flanges place material far from the center of the section, where it adds the most stiffness

questions.explanation: A beam's stiffness depends on depth cubed, so material far from the neutral axis is more valuable than material near it. An 11⅞ in. I-joist has about 164 in⁴ and 8.6 in² of wood, versus 178 in⁴ and 16.9 in² for the sawn 2×12. Its web is OSB, not steel, and cross-lamination describes plywood and CLT rather than flanges.

questions.question_text: Why are framing members commonly spaced at 16 or 24 in. on center?

options.A: Both match the minimum spacing the code allows between studs in bearing walls
options.B: Both keep the studs far enough apart to eliminate thermal bridging
options.C: Both divide 48 in. evenly, so they match the 4 ft by 8 ft sheathing panels
options.D: Both are the only spacings at which light-frame wood walls can resist wind

questions.explanation: Light-frame wood construction uses closely spaced studs, joists, and rafters or trusses covered with sheathing, and the spacing is chosen so panel edges fall on framing members. The numerous members make the system redundant: a weak stud shares its load through the sheathing. Spacing does not eliminate thermal bridging, and other spacings can resist wind.

questions.question_text: How does OSB differ in construction from plywood?

options.A: OSB is made of veneers with parallel grain, while plywood is made of strands aligned in a single direction under heat
options.B: OSB is made of wood strands aligned in layers and bonded with resin, while plywood is veneers with alternating grain
options.C: OSB is made of finger-jointed laminations, while plywood is made of crossing boards
options.D: OSB is a hardwood product used only for finishes, while plywood is a softwood used only for framing work

questions.explanation: Plywood is thin veneers peeled from a log and glued with each layer perpendicular to its neighbors, which makes it nearly equal in strength in both directions. OSB uses long strands in oriented layers, bonded under heat and pressure. Both are 4 ft by 8 ft structural sheathing panels with a span rating, and OSB edges can swell if soaked.

questions.question_text: A roof has an 8:12 pitch. How much does it rise over a horizontal run of 9 ft?

options.B: 4.5 ft
options.C: 6.0 ft
options.D: 8.0 ft

questions.explanation: Roof pitch is the rise in inches per 12 in. of run, so rise = run × 8/12 = 9 × 8/12 = 6.0 ft. The value 13.5 ft inverts the ratio, 4.5 ft uses a 6:12 slope, and 8.0 ft takes the pitch number as feet. Knowing the rise lets you find rafter length with the Pythagorean theorem and order lumber in standard lengths.

questions.question_text: Why is structural steel usually protected with fireproofing and coatings even though it is strong, stiff, and ductile?

options.A: It burns in a fire because it is combustible, and it swells when exposed to moisture
options.B: It loses strength at temperatures reached in a building fire and corrodes without coatings
options.C: It cannot carry compression after yielding, and it conducts too little heat to dissipate fire
options.D: It shrinks as it dries, so cladding attached to steel would crack over time

questions.explanation: Steel is an alloy with a modulus of about 29,000 ksi and yield strength of 36 to 50 ksi, and it gives warning of overload by stretching. Its weaknesses are loss of strength in fire, which is why it gets sprayed-on fireproofing, intumescent paint, or gypsum enclosures, and corrosion. It is noncombustible and conducts heat well, so it is also an effective thermal bridge.

questions.question_text: What is the main trade-off of platform framing compared with balloon framing?

options.A: Each platform lets studs run continuously, but fire can spread freely through the open wall cavities above
options.B: Each platform reduces shrinkage to zero, but workers lack a safe surface from which to build the next story
options.C: Each platform lowers the cost of walls, but joists carry no load from the framing above
options.D: Each platform interrupts vertical fire paths, but horizontal-grain wood at every floor adds cumulative shrinkage

questions.explanation: In platform framing each story is a separate platform, so the floor interrupts cavities that let fire race upward and gives workers a safe surface. The joist and plates have their grain horizontal, so they shrink in height as they dry; about 0.28 in. per floor in the example, or 0.83 in. over three floors. Balloon framing ran studs continuously through all floors.

questions.question_text: Which set of functions describes wall studs?

options.A: They carry vertical loads, resist wind pressure by spanning between floors, and provide nailing for sheathing
options.B: They span openings to carry loads around them, and they are sized from the code's span tables for houses
options.C: They tie the roof to the walls and resist uplift from wind suction, using metal straps and screws
options.D: They support the subfloor and keep the floor from bouncing under foot traffic across the joist span

questions.explanation: Studs are the vertical members of a framed wall, typically 2×4 or 2×6 at 16 or 24 in. on center. A 2×6 gives a deeper cavity for insulation, so many Minnesota exterior walls use them. Spanning openings is the job of headers, tying roofs to walls is done by metal straps, and supporting the floor is the job of joists and the subfloor.

questions.question_text: Why is glulam stronger than sawn lumber of the same size?

options.A: Defects are scattered across many laminations, and the best lumber goes at top and bottom where bending stress peaks
options.B: Its laminations run perpendicular to one another, so each layer reinforces the layers above and below it in bending
options.C: Its laminations are made of steel-reinforced veneers that carry the bending stresses
options.D: Its adhesive is stronger than the lumber itself, so the member can never fail along its glue lines

questions.explanation: Glulam bonds many layers of lumber face-to-face with the grain of every layer along the length, and finger joints allow members much longer than a single board. Because knots are scattered and top and bottom laminations hold the best lumber, it outperforms sawn lumber. Crossing layers describe CLT, not glulam, and large glulam members also char slowly in a fire.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes cross-laminated timber?

options.A: A beam of thin veneers glued with parallel grain, used as headers and girders in framed buildings
options.B: A panel of oriented wood strands bonded in layers, used mainly as wall and roof sheathing
options.C: A large panel of boards in perpendicular glued layers, used as a floor, wall, or roof panel
options.D: A member of finger-jointed laminations bent into curves, used for arches and gymnasium beams

questions.explanation: CLT typically has three, five, or seven layers, each perpendicular to the one beneath, so the panel carries load in both directions like a thick plate. It is cut and prepared in a factory and erected by crane, and it belongs to the mass timber group. The parallel-veneer product is LVL, the strand panel is OSB, and the curved member is glulam.

questions.question_text: A wood sample weighs 48 g as delivered and 40 g after oven drying. What is its moisture content?

options.A: 16.7 percent
options.B: 8 percent
options.C: 120 percent
options.D: 20 percent

questions.explanation: Moisture content is the mass of water divided by the oven-dry mass: (48 − 40) / 40 = 0.20, or 20 percent. Dividing by the wet mass gives 16.7 percent, which understates it. The value 8 is the water mass in grams, not a percentage, and 120 percent divides the wet mass by the dry mass. At a sustained 20 percent, decay fungi can begin to grow.

questions.question_text: A W14×30 wide-flange beam is 30 ft long. About how much does the beam weigh?

options.A: 420 lb
options.B: 900 lb
options.C: 14 lb
options.D: 30 lb

questions.explanation: The designation names a wide-flange shape about 14 in. deep that weighs 30 lb per foot, so weight = 30 lb/ft × 30 ft = 900 lb. Multiplying the depth by the length gives 420, which treats the depth as the weight. The values 14 and 30 lb are only single numbers from the name, and the beam's dead load follows from weight per foot times length.

questions.question_text: In the framing around a window opening, which members carry the header's load down to the floor framing and foundation?

options.A: Cripple studs, which fill the short spaces above the header
options.B: King studs, which run the full height of the wall
options.C: Sole plates, which run along the bottom of the wall
options.D: Jack studs, also called trimmers, at each end of the header

questions.explanation: A header is a beam over an opening that carries loads around it. Jack studs stand at each end of the header and support it. King studs run the full wall height beside them to tie the opening to the plates and brace it against wind, and cripple studs fill the short spaces above the header and below a sill. Plates do not support the header's concentrated end loads.

questions.question_text: Why do stiffness and vibration, rather than strength, usually decide joist size in a wood floor?

options.A: Wood joists are always strong enough, so no strength check is ever needed
options.B: Subfloors carry most of the load, so joists do not need to resist bending
options.C: Occupants notice a bouncy floor long before it threatens collapse
options.D: Codes limit joist spans only by stiffness and not by any strength requirement

questions.explanation: A floor system is joists or trusses with a subfloor, and strength is rarely the controlling issue. A floor that sags or bounces is unacceptable even if it never breaks, so deflection and vibration limits set the member size. Strength must still be checked, and the floor also acts as the horizontal diaphragm that collects lateral loads and passes them to shear walls.

questions.question_text: How does a slip-critical bolted connection carry load differently from a bearing-type connection?

options.A: The bolts are tightened snug so the shank presses on the sides of the hole and carries the load
options.B: The bolts are tightened to a specified high tension, so friction between clamped plates carries the load
options.C: The bolts are welded to the plates, so the load passes through the weld and not through the bolts
options.D: The bolts are left loose, so the plates can slip until they bear against the nut and washer

questions.explanation: In a bearing-type connection the bolts are snug and load passes from plate to plate as the shank bears on the hole. In a slip-critical connection the plates are clamped together and friction carries the load. Bolts are the common choice for field connections because ordinary wrenches work in any weather, and holes are slightly oversized for erection tolerance.

questions.question_text: Why are most structural welds made in the fabricator's shop, with the pieces then bolted together on site?

options.A: Shop conditions are controlled, while field welding needs qualified welders, inspection, and preheating in cold
options.B: Shop welds are always stronger than any bolted joint, so no site connection is ever needed in the building
options.C: Bolts cannot be tightened in cold weather, so field welding is the only option for connections made on site
options.D: Welding is allowed only on plates and never on beams, so the shop prepares plates and the field bolts beams

questions.explanation: A weld melts the edges of the metal with filler so the joint becomes continuous steel. Controlled shop conditions help quality, while field welds, used where a rigid connection such as a moment frame is needed, require qualified welders and visual or ultrasonic inspection. In cold weather, steel is preheated to avoid cracking. Bolts can be installed in any weather with ordinary wrenches.

questions.question_text: A designer proposes a Minnesota exterior wall of light-gauge steel studs filled only with cavity insulation. What concern does this raise and what is the usual remedy?

options.A: Steel studs absorb moisture and rot, so the cavity must be filled with a vapor barrier on both faces
options.B: Steel conducts heat so well that studs bridge the insulation, so continuous insulation goes outside the framing
options.C: Steel studs shrink as they dry, so the sheathing must be spaced to allow for movement in the wall
options.D: Steel studs burn at low temperatures, so gypsum must be added to every cavity of the wall assembly

questions.explanation: Light-gauge steel studs are cold-bent C-shapes in the same arrangement as wood framing. They do not burn, rot, shrink, or attract termites, but steel conducts heat several hundred times as readily as wood, so cavity insulation loses much of its effectiveness. Cold climates therefore need continuous insulation outside the framing, a strategy covered in Chapter 11.

questions.question_text: What does composite floor deck provide that ordinary roof deck does not?

options.A: A deeper profile that allows it to span between columns without any supporting beams
options.B: A coating that makes the deck noncombustible and eliminates the need for fire protection
options.C: Embossments that bond to a poured concrete topping so the deck and slab act together
options.D: A wood layer that serves as a nailing surface for the floor finishes above it

questions.explanation: Steel decking is corrugated sheet steel that spans between joists or beams. Roof deck is about 1½ in. deep and carries roofing and insulation, while composite floor deck has a deeper profile with embossments so that the concrete topping bonds to it. Fastened by welds or screws, any deck also acts as the horizontal diaphragm that carries wind and seismic forces.

questions.question_text: Why can concrete harden under water, and why does concrete that dries out too early stop gaining strength?

options.A: It hardens by evaporation of the mixing water, so a wet environment only slows the process down
options.B: It hardens by cooling of the cement paste, so added water speeds up the change of state
options.C: It hardens by hydration, a chemical reaction that needs moisture, so drying out stops the reaction
options.D: It hardens by compaction of the aggregates, so moisture only affects the surface finish of the slab

questions.explanation: Hydration is the combination of cement with water to form interlocking crystals that bind the mixture. It releases heat and continues for weeks, as long as moisture and moderate temperatures are available. Hydration is not drying, so water is an ingredient and not a solvent that must leave. Concrete that dries too early stops gaining strength, which is why the goal after the pour is keeping the water in.

questions.question_text: What is the role of cement in concrete?

options.A: It is the granular material that makes up most of the volume and limits shrinkage of the paste
options.B: It is the binder that reacts with water to form a paste that glues the aggregates together
options.C: It is the steel that carries the tension the concrete cannot carry on its own in a beam
options.D: It is the chemical added in small doses to change the workability or the set time of a mix

questions.explanation: Portland cement is made by heating limestone and clay in a kiln and grinding the clinker with a little gypsum. It reacts with water in hydration, so cement is the glue and not the product. A sidewalk is concrete, never cement. The granular material is aggregate, the tension carrier is rebar, and the small-dose chemicals are admixtures.

questions.question_text: A #4 reinforcing bar has a cross-sectional area of 0.20 in² and a yield strength of 60 ksi. About how much tension can it carry at yield?

options.A: 0.33 kips
options.B: 120 kips
options.C: 60 kips
options.D: 12 kips

questions.explanation: Force equals area times stress: 0.20 in² × 60 ksi = 12 kips. The value 0.33 kips divides the stress by the area, 120 kips overstates by a factor of ten, and 60 kips simply repeats the yield strength. Rebar provides in a thin bar the tension capacity that concrete, at about 10 percent of its compressive strength, cannot provide at all.

questions.question_text: In masonry vocabulary, what is a wythe?

options.A: A vertical layer of masonry one unit thick
options.B: A horizontal layer of units laid in a wall
options.C: The pattern in which vertical joints are staggered
options.D: The thin facing of brick attached to a structural backup

questions.explanation: A course is a horizontal layer of units, a wythe is a vertical layer one unit thick, and the bond is the pattern in which vertical joints are staggered from course to course, commonly running bond. A thin facing attached to a structural backup is a veneer. Masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension, like concrete.

questions.question_text: A wall form has a narrowest dimension of 8 in., rebar with a 3 in. clear spacing, and an adjoining slab 6 in. deep. Using the one-fifth, three-quarters, and one-third rules, what maximum aggregate size controls?

options.A: 2.0 in., from one-third of the 6 in. slab depth
options.B: 2.25 in., from three-quarters of the clear bar spacing
options.C: 3.0 in., from the clear spacing between the bars
options.D: 1.6 in., from one-fifth of the narrowest form dimension

questions.explanation: The limits are 8/5 = 1.6 in. for the form, 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 in. for the bars, and 6/3 = 2.0 in. for the slab. The smallest result controls, because a larger stone would jam and leave voids. Aggregates make up 60 to 75 percent of concrete's volume and should be hard, clean, and well graded.

questions.question_text: A concrete mix contains 600 lb of cement and 270 lb of water per cubic yard. What is its water-cement ratio?
questions.explanation: The water-cement ratio is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement: 270 / 600 = 0.45. The value 2.22 inverts the ratio, and 0.25 is only about what hydration itself needs by mass. A lower ratio produces stronger, denser, less permeable concrete, and exposed Minnesota concrete commonly needs 0.45 or lower, so adding water at the chute can push it out of specification.

questions.question_text: In the absolute volume method of mix design, why does the aggregate volume equal whatever remains after the other ingredients are accounted for?

options.A: The aggregate must always make up exactly 60 percent of the mix by mass
options.B: The masses of all ingredients must add up to 27 lb per cubic foot of concrete
options.C: The solid volumes of all ingredients must add up to exactly 27 ft³, one cubic yard
options.D: The cement and water must fill all of the space that the air does not occupy

questions.explanation: Absolute volume is bookkeeping: each ingredient's volume is its mass divided by its specific gravity times 62.4 lb/ft³, and the totals must equal 27 ft³. In the example, cement, water, and air take 8.56 ft³, so the aggregate fills 18.44 ft³. Aggregates usually occupy 60 to 75 percent of the volume, and the mix's mass totals thousands of pounds, not 27.

questions.question_text: Why do form designers either space ties closer together or use stronger ties near the bottom of a tall wall pour?

options.A: Concrete hardens first at the bottom, so the ties must resist its early shrinkage
options.B: Fresh concrete acts like a heavy liquid, so pressure on the form increases with depth
options.C: The top of the pour carries the weight of the crew, so the bottom must be braced
options.D: Vibration is applied only at the base, so the pressure there is higher than anywhere else

questions.explanation: Fresh concrete behaves like a fluid, so the pressure at the base of an 8 ft pour is at most about 150 × 8 = 1,200 psf, falling to zero at the top. A tie one foot above the base on a 2 ft grid could see about 4,200 lb. A form designed for less than full fluid pressure can burst. Slower pours and cooler concrete reduce the actual pressure.

questions.question_text: Which three reasons explain why steel and concrete work well together in reinforced concrete?

options.A: Deformed bars bond to the concrete, both expand by nearly the same amount, and concrete's alkalinity protects steel from rust
options.B: Steel is lighter than concrete, both have the same tensile strength, and concrete's porosity absorbs the steel's heat
options.C: Steel stiffens the aggregates, both shrink at the same rate, and concrete's acidity cleans the steel surface of rust
options.D: Steel is cheaper than concrete, both resist compression equally, and concrete's moisture hydrates the steel bars

questions.explanation: Ribs on deformed bars create a strong bond, steel and concrete expand about 6 millionths per °F so they do not pull apart with the seasons, and concrete forms a protective film on steel as long as it stays sound. Concrete is weak in tension, steel is strong in tension, and the partnership assigns compression to concrete and tension to steel.

questions.question_text: Why should concrete be placed close to its final position instead of being dropped from a great height or pushed far?

options.A: Dropping it speeds hydration, so the concrete sets before it can be consolidated
options.B: Dropping or pushing it can segregate the mix, so the stone separates from the paste
options.C: Pushing it allows air bubbles to escape, so the concrete loses its freeze-thaw resistance
options.D: Dropping it adds water to the mix, so the water-cement ratio rises

questions.explanation: Placement delivers fresh concrete to the forms, spreads it, consolidates it, and finishes it. Segregation weakens the mix. Concrete is also normally discharged within about 90 minutes of mixing because hydration has begun. Consolidation with an internal vibrator releases trapped air, and under-vibration leaves honeycombing while over-vibration causes segregation.

questions.question_text: What is the main advantage of cast-in-place concrete compared with assembled precast pieces?

options.A: The concrete is cured in a factory, so its quality does not depend on site weather or labor
options.B: The forms are not required, so the pour can proceed immediately after the excavation is complete
options.C: The reinforcement is eliminated, because the concrete cures in its final position in the building
options.D: The pieces form a single monolithic structure that can carry moment connections and unusual shapes

questions.explanation: Cast-in-place concrete is placed and cured in its final location in forms built on site, which makes it monolithic. Its disadvantages are dependence on weather, site labor, and time, since each pour must cure before it is loaded. Factory curing describes precast, and forms and reinforcement are always needed for cast-in-place work.

questions.question_text: From the top down, what is the order of layers in a typical slab on grade in a cold climate?

options.A: Concrete slab, rigid insulation, compacted subgrade, vapor retarder, compacted granular base
options.B: Vapor retarder, concrete slab, compacted granular base, rigid insulation, compacted subgrade
options.C: Concrete slab, vapor retarder, rigid insulation where needed, granular base, compacted subgrade
options.D: Compacted subgrade, compacted granular base, concrete slab, rigid insulation, vapor retarder

questions.explanation: A slab on grade rests directly on soil. The vapor retarder sits beneath the slab to block ground moisture, rigid insulation keeps the ground from drawing heat away, and the compacted granular base rests on the compacted subgrade prepared during site work. A suspended slab, by contrast, spans between beams or walls as a structural member and needs reinforcement.

questions.question_text: Why is mortar deliberately made a little weaker and more flexible than the masonry units?

options.A: Weaker mortar bonds better to the units, so it prevents any cracking from forming in the wall
options.B: Any cracking then occurs in the joint, which can be repaired by repointing, not by replacing units
options.C: Weaker mortar hydrates faster, so the wall can be loaded sooner after construction is complete
options.D: Flexible mortar absorbs all of the wall's compressive load, so the units themselves can be thinner

questions.explanation: Mortar bonds the units and seals the joints, and standard types M, S, N, and O range from 2,500 psi down to 350 psi minimum. Type N is common above grade, and Type S is used where higher bond or lateral strength is needed. A softer joint localizes cracks where they can be tooled and repointed. Mortar does not carry all the load, and weakness is a design choice, not a way to prevent cracking.

questions.question_text: A modular brick face needs about 6.75 bricks per square foot of wall. About how many bricks are needed for a 100 ft² wall, before any allowance for breakage?

options.A: 675 bricks
options.B: 15 bricks
options.C: 1,440 bricks
options.D: 6,750 bricks

questions.explanation: Multiply the bricks per square foot by the wall area: 100 × 6.75 = 675. The value 15 divides the area by 6.75, 1,440 treats the wall as 144 ft², and 6,750 is a decimal-place error. A typical estimate then adds an allowance such as 5 percent for breakage. Minnesota brick exposed to the weather should be Grade SW, severe weathering.

questions.question_text: Which description of a standard concrete masonry unit is correct?

options.A: Nominally 4 in. by 2⅔ in. by 8 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. more in each direction, solid sides, and no cores
options.B: Nominally 8 in. by 8 in. by 16 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. more in each direction and no hollow cores
options.C: Nominally 8 by 8 by 16 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. less in each direction and hollow cores that can be grouted
options.D: Nominally 12 in. by 12 in. by 24 in., with an actual size equal to the nominal size and a solid face

questions.explanation: CMUs are hollow or solid units of molded concrete. The actual size is ⅜ in. smaller than nominal in each direction so that the unit plus its mortar joint fits the module. The cores reduce weight and can be filled with grout and rebar, and the thick sides are called face shells. The 4 × 2⅔ × 8 module describes brick with its joint.

questions.question_text: Why is grout made much more fluid than ordinary concrete, with a slump of 8 to 11 in.?

options.A: It must evaporate quickly from the cores so that the units can be loaded on the same day
options.B: It must stay on the surface of the wall to seal the mortar joints against wind-driven rain
options.C: It must replace the mortar, so it fills each joint without any other bonding agent being used
options.D: It must flow into narrow block cores and around bars to bond the steel and add strength

questions.explanation: Grout is a concrete-like mixture of cement, fine aggregate or pea gravel, and water poured into the cores of concrete blocks or between wythes. It is consolidated by vibrator or puddling and placed in lifts of limited height so the pressure does not blow out the block face shells. Mortar bonds units and seals joints, while grout bonds steel and strengthens cells.

questions.question_text: A slab is finished on a hot, dry, windy afternoon, and fine cracks appear within hours. What practice would best prevent this problem?

options.A: Let the surface dry quickly so that the excess water leaves the slab before hydration begins
options.B: Add water to the surface as it stiffens so the finish stays workable for the finishing crew
options.C: Wait for the 28-day cylinder results to come back before beginning any curing of the slab
options.D: Keep the surface moist from the start with curing compound, wet burlap, or plastic sheeting

questions.explanation: Hot, dry, or windy conditions pull water from the surface faster than it rises from within, causing plastic shrinkage cracks. Curing keeps freshly placed concrete moist and in a suitable temperature range so hydration continues and the concrete reaches its design strength. Moist curing is commonly required for at least seven days, and adding surface water or waiting for tests does not protect the slab.

questions.question_text: A contractor wants to core-drill an unmarked post-tensioned slab without locating the tendons first. Why is this dangerous?

options.A: The tendons carry no load, so drilling through them only damages the slab's insulation layer
options.B: The tendons hold great stored energy, so cutting one can cause a violent release and weaken the slab
options.C: The tendons are made of brittle cast iron, so drilling shatters the concrete around them
options.D: The tendons are filled with grout under pressure, so drilling releases wet concrete into the room below

questions.explanation: In post-tensioning, high-strength strands run through ducts and are stretched with jacks after the concrete hardens, which keeps the concrete in compression before loads arrive. That stored energy is why an unmarked post-tensioned slab must never be cut or drilled until tendons are located. Prestressing allows longer spans and thinner slabs, as in parking structures and office floors.

questions.question_text: What are the main advantages and limits of precast concrete?

options.A: Pieces are cast in their final positions on site, but weather and labor affect quality and schedule
options.B: Pieces are always unreinforced, but they are cheaper than any cast-in-place alternative at any size
options.C: Factory conditions give precise forms and consistent quality, but size limits and critical connections apply
options.D: Pieces are poured on the building's own slab, but they cannot be lifted by a crane or tilted up

questions.explanation: Precast concrete is cast in a plant and lifted into place, so it has precise forms and controlled curing regardless of weather, and many pieces are also prestressed. Hollow-core planks, double-tee beams, wall panels, beams, and columns are common. Connections between pieces, made by welded plates, bolts, or grouted joints, are critical details. Casting on the building's slab describes tilt-up construction.

questions.question_text: Why is reinforced masonry the standard way to build a masonry shear wall?

options.A: Unreinforced masonry is brittle and weak against sideways forces, and grouted bars let the wall resist tension and shear
options.B: Unreinforced masonry is too heavy for lateral loads, and grouted bars reduce the wall's weight enough to resist them
options.C: Unreinforced masonry cannot resist compression, and grouted bars carry the vertical load of the floors above
options.D: Unreinforced masonry is not fire resistant, and grouted bars supply the fire-resistance rating of the wall

questions.explanation: Reinforced masonry places steel bars or wires in grout-filled cells or joints. Vertical bars go at corners, openings, and regular spacing; bond beams tie courses together; and joint reinforcement controls cracking. Masonry is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel is needed where wind or seismic forces are significant. Masonry is already heavy and fire resistant.

questions.question_text: How is stone masonry used in modern buildings?

options.A: Mainly as thick walls that carry load by their weight alone, as in historic buildings and old mills
options.B: Mainly as rough rubble placed in the forms to replace the aggregates in a concrete mix
options.C: Mainly as a thin veneer anchored to a backup wall, with anchorage designed for the stone's weight
options.D: Mainly as lightweight panels that weigh less than 50 pcf and are glued to the wall surface

questions.explanation: Historic buildings used very thick stone walls carrying load by weight, but modern buildings use stone mostly as veneer. Stone weighs roughly 150 to 170 pcf, so anchorage must be designed for that weight, and the stone must be chosen for its resistance to freezing when wet. Common building stones include granite, limestone, and sandstone, and Minnesota has quarried limestone and granite for generations.

questions.question_text: Using the rule of 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in inches, expressed in feet, what spacing of control joints is appropriate for a 6 in. slab?

options.A: 6 to 9 ft
options.B: 24 to 36 ft
options.C: 2 to 3 ft
options.D: 12 to 18 ft

questions.explanation: The rule multiplies the thickness in inches by 2 to 3 and reads the answer in feet: 6 × 2 = 12 ft and 6 × 3 = 18 ft. A control joint is a deliberately weakened line, sawn to about one-quarter of the slab depth within hours of finishing, that directs shrinkage cracking to a straight, controlled line. A restrained slab would otherwise crack at random.

questions.question_text: What does the rule "clay expands and concrete shrinks" imply for joints in a brick veneer over a concrete block backup?

options.A: Brick veneer needs control joints directing its shrinkage cracks, while concrete block needs full-depth expansion joints
options.B: Brick veneer needs full-depth expansion joints, while concrete block needs control joints directing shrinkage cracks
options.C: Neither material needs joints, because both change size by the same amount with temperature and moisture
options.D: Both materials need only expansion joints, because both of them shrink as they dry and then stay stable

questions.explanation: Clay brick expands slowly over its life as it absorbs moisture, while concrete products shrink as they dry. An expansion joint is a full-depth gap with compressible filler that lets two parts move independently, and it divides long runs of brick veneer. A control joint is a partial-depth weakened line that directs shrinkage cracks, which suits concrete and block.

questions.question_text: A lot is 200 ft wide and 150 ft deep. Zoning requires setbacks of 10 ft on each side, 25 ft at the front, and 15 ft at the rear. What is the area of the buildable envelope?
questions.explanation: The envelope's width is 200 − 10 − 10 = 180 ft, and its depth is 150 − 25 − 15 = 110 ft, so the area is 180 × 110 = 19,800 ft². The lot area (30,000) ignores all setbacks, 27,000 ignores the front and rear setbacks, and 22,500 ignores the rear setback. Easements, wetlands, or steep slopes would shrink the usable area further.

questions.question_text: A sieve analysis finds 5 percent gravel, 25 percent sand, and 70 percent fines of low plasticity. Which classification and behavior fit best?

options.A: A coarse-grained silty sand with good drainage, high strength, and low frost susceptibility
options.B: A well-graded gravel with excellent bearing capacity and excellent drainage
options.C: A fine-grained, silt-like soil with poor drainage and very high frost susceptibility
options.D: An organic soil that is very strong when saturated and easy to compact in lifts

questions.explanation: Fines are particles smaller than 0.075 mm that pass the No. 200 sieve. When more than half of a sample passes it, the soil is fine-grained. With low-plasticity fines, the soil behaves like a silt: poor drainage, low to moderate strength, strength lost when saturated, and very high frost susceptibility. The coarse-grained options contradict the 70 percent fines, and organic soil is weak and compressible.

questions.question_text: A column carries 60 kips and the soil's allowable bearing capacity is 2,000 psf. What footing area is required?

options.A: 30 ft²
options.B: 3 ft²
options.C: 60 ft²
options.D: 120 ft²

questions.explanation: Required area equals load divided by allowable bearing capacity: 60,000 lb / 2,000 psf = 30 ft², about 5.5 ft square. The value 3 ft² comes from using kips against psf with the wrong decimal, and 60 and 120 ft² use capacities of 1,000 and 500 psf. Weaker soil demands a larger footing, and a real design also adds the footing's own weight.

questions.question_text: A crew strips topsoil from the whole building pad before installing any silt fence. What problem does this sequence invite?

options.A: Compaction of the topsoil by the equipment, which makes the stockpile unusable for later landscaping
options.B: Loss of the utility markings, which are removed along with the topsoil layer during stripping
options.C: Settlement of the future footings, which would rest on the thin layer of topsoil left behind
options.D: Bare soil with no sediment control, which can wash off the site in the first rain and draw a stop-work order

questions.explanation: Preparation is as much about protecting the surroundings as changing the land. The recommended order is to locate utilities, survey, install erosion and sediment controls, protect what stays, then clear, grub, and strip. Stripping first exposes bare soil with nothing to stop runoff, which is the most common sequencing mistake. Topsoil is stripped because it is unsuitable for supporting a building.

questions.question_text: An excavation removes 300 yd³ of soil measured in place (bank volume). With a swell factor of 25 percent, what loose volume must the trucks haul?

options.A: 240 yd³
options.B: 325 yd³
options.C: 375 yd³
options.D: 300 yd³

questions.explanation: Once dug, soil is loosened and occupies more space. The loose volume is the bank volume times (1 + swell factor): 300 × 1.25 = 375 yd³. Dividing by 1.25 gives 240 yd³, adding 25 yd³ gives 325, and 300 ignores swell entirely. Quantities should be tracked separately as bank, loose, and compacted volumes, because compacted fill shrinks again.

questions.question_text: Why should below-grade space be designed for the seasonal high water level and not the water level observed on the day of the borings?

options.A: The water table rises with spring snowmelt and rain, and a dry-season boring can read too low
options.B: The water table stays constant all year, so any boring date gives a reliable value for design
options.C: Groundwater only exerts pressure in spring, so the other seasons are not important for design
options.D: Saturated soil is stronger than dry soil, so the high level is the safest assumption for bearing

questions.explanation: Groundwater fills the spaces between soil particles below the water table, and hydrostatic pressure increases by about 62.4 psf per foot of depth. A slab 6 ft below the water table sees about 374 psf of uplift, which can crack and lift it. Saturated soil is usually weaker, not stronger, and the water table varies with season.

questions.question_text: An entry sits at elevation 100.00 ft and the parking lot edge, 50 ft away, is at 98.50 ft. What is the walk's slope, and how does it compare with the 5 percent threshold between a walk and a ramp?

options.A: 3 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it must be treated as a ramp
options.B: 3 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it remains a regular walking route
options.C: 33 percent, which is above 5 percent, so it must be treated as a ramp
options.D: 0.03 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it needs no slope at all

questions.explanation: The drop is 1.5 ft over 50 ft, or 0.03, which is 3 percent. Accessibility standards generally treat a walking surface steeper than 1:20 (5 percent) as a ramp with additional requirements, so this walk is a regular route. The value 33 percent inverts the ratio. Codes also commonly require ground to fall at least 6 in within the first 10 ft away from the foundation.

questions.question_text: What is the practical purpose of the code's frost depth requirement for exterior footings?

options.A: It places the bottom of footings at the depth where the water table is found in spring
options.B: It places the bottom of footings at the depth where the soil changes from silt to granular
options.C: It places the bottom of footings above frozen soil so they can be inspected in winter
options.D: It places the bottom of footings below the depth to which ground freezes in a severe winter

questions.explanation: Frost depth is the depth to which the ground freezes, and the code sets a minimum depth for the bottoms of footings so they sit below frozen soil. In the Twin Cities area it is commonly 42 inches and greater farther north, but the local building official establishes the project value. It records the deepest freezing expected in a severe winter, not the frost line seen on a single cold morning.

questions.question_text: What does a French drain do?

options.A: It uses perforated pipe in gravel to intercept groundwater
options.B: It uses a shallow vegetated channel to carry surface water away from pavement
options.C: It uses an inlet in the pavement to collect surface runoff
options.D: It uses a basin to hold stormwater and release it slowly

questions.explanation: Subsurface drainage uses perforated pipe in gravel to intercept groundwater. Surface drainage uses grading, swales (shallow vegetated channels), catch basins (pavement inlets), and storm sewers. Municipalities and watershed districts commonly require basins that hold back stormwater and release it slowly so downstream flooding does not increase.

questions.question_text: Why does the geotechnical investigation order borings early, during schematic design, rather than after the foundation is drawn?

options.A: Borings are cheaper in schematic design because the soil is easier to sample before drawings begin
options.B: The code requires foundation plans to be drawn before the soil's allowable bearing capacity is known
options.C: The standard penetration test cannot be performed once the building footprint is staked
options.D: A report that arrives first can guide where the building goes, while a late report can force a redesign

questions.explanation: Soil testing combines field exploration and laboratory analysis, directed by a geotechnical engineer, and replaces assumptions with data on grain size, Atterberg limits, moisture, and compaction. The report recommends allowable bearing capacity and records frost and groundwater observations. Borings are a small fraction of the project budget and protect against the largest foundation unknowns.

questions.question_text: A slab edge rises each winter over wet silt. Which measure removes one of the three conditions needed for frost heave?

options.A: Add a second layer of concrete to increase the slab's weight
options.B: Replace the silt beneath the slab edge with clean gravel
options.C: Seal the slab surface so snow cannot melt onto it
options.D: Increase the slab thickness so the freezing front cannot reach it

questions.explanation: Frost heave requires frost-susceptible soil, a supply of water, and freezing temperatures together. The main cause is the growth of ice lenses as freezing soil draws water upward by capillary action. Silt is the worst offender. Removing any one condition stops heave, so options include footings below frost depth, replacing silty soil with clean gravel, or draining the water away.

questions.question_text: A geotechnical report finds 15 ft of soft peat above firm sand beneath a light building. Which foundation recommendation follows the chapter's logic?

options.A: Spread footings bearing on the peat at the frost depth
options.B: Piles that pass through the peat to bear in the firm sand
options.C: Wider continuous footings placed on the peat surface
options.D: A thicker slab-on-grade placed directly on the peat

questions.explanation: A foundation spreads load over enough soil that the soil is not overstressed. Designers begin with the cheapest option that works, almost always shallow, and move deeper only when soil forces them to. Shallow footings on 15 ft of soft peat would settle badly, so deep foundations that reach firm soil below the weak layer are needed. The decision follows the soil.

questions.question_text: Why does a "shallow" exterior footing in Minneapolis still sit more than 3 ft below the surface?

options.A: Shallow describes the depth of the concrete, and Minnesota soil requires a minimum of 3 ft for all footings
options.B: Shallow footings must reach the water table so that groundwater supports the building
options.C: Shallow footings must sit below the topsoil, which is always at least 3 ft deep
options.D: Shallow describes how load reaches the soil, and the bottom must sit below frost depth, commonly 42 in

questions.explanation: Shallow foundations carry load to soil near the surface through a footing wider than the wall or column above it. The word does not refer to the concrete's depth, and frost depth sets it for exterior footings. Frost depth governs the depth, and bearing capacity governs the width. An interior footing in a heated building may not need the frost rule.

questions.question_text: A bearing wall delivers 3,000 plf to soil with an allowable bearing capacity of 2,000 psf. What footing width is required?

options.A: 18 in
options.B: 8 in
options.C: 36 in
options.D: 1.5 in

questions.explanation: The required width equals line load divided by allowable pressure: 3,000 / 2,000 = 1.5 ft, which is 18 in. Dividing the other way gives 0.67 ft (8 in), 36 in doubles the answer, and 1.5 in confuses feet with inches. Footing thickness is set separately, commonly 8 in or more for a light-frame building, so the footing is stiff enough to spread the load without cracking.

questions.question_text: A 9 ft basement wall retains soil with an equivalent fluid pressure of 40 pcf. What is the lateral force per foot of wall?

options.A: 360 lb per foot
options.B: 3,240 lb per foot
options.C: 1,620 lb per foot
options.D: 540 lb per foot

questions.explanation: The force is the area of the pressure triangle: F = ½ γ_e h² = 0.5 × 40 × 81 = 1,620 lb per foot, acting one third of the height above the base. The value 360 psf is only the pressure at the base, 3,240 omits the one-half, and 540 mixes up the height. A foundation wall carries the vertical load of the wall above and also resists this lateral pressure.

questions.question_text: In what two ways does a deep foundation element resist load?

options.A: Footing spread at the base and mat action across the top
options.B: Hydrostatic uplift and perimeter drainage of the walls
options.C: End bearing at the tip and skin friction along the sides
options.D: Frost heave and lateral soil pressure on the walls

questions.explanation: Deep foundations pass through weak layers to firmer soil or rock. End bearing is the load carried by the tip pressing on firm soil or rock, and skin friction is the load carried by friction along the sides. A pile cap, a concrete block over a group of piles, ties them together and receives the column load. The other pairs describe shallow foundations or soil forces.

questions.question_text: A square spread footing 5 ft on a side carries a 45 kip column load. What average pressure does it place on the soil?

options.C: 225 psf

questions.explanation: Pressure equals load divided by bearing area: 45,000 lb / (5 ft × 5 ft) = 45,000 / 25 = 1,800 psf. Dividing by the 5 ft side alone gives 9,000, 225 divides by 200 ft², and 11,250 divides by only 4 ft². Spread footings are common under steel columns and under posts that support glulam beams.

questions.question_text: Why are basements common in cold climates?

options.A: Footings must go deep for frost anyway, so the added excavation yields usable space cheaply
options.B: Basements are required by code in any region where the ground freezes to a depth of 3 ft
options.C: Basements eliminate the groundwater and radon problems that slab floors face in cold regions
options.D: Basements allow the footings to be placed above the frost depth, saving excavation and concrete

questions.explanation: A basement is a story partly or fully below grade, enclosed by foundation walls. It adds living or storage space, houses mechanical equipment, and keeps the floor above cold ground. It also takes on groundwater, radon, and moisture problems, and habitable basement rooms need an emergency escape opening. Footings still must reach below frost depth.

questions.question_text: From the bottom up, what is the typical order of layers in a slab-on-grade?

options.A: Concrete slab, vapor retarder, granular base, compacted subgrade
options.B: Granular base, compacted subgrade, concrete slab, vapor retarder
options.C: Compacted subgrade, vapor retarder, concrete slab, granular base
options.D: Compacted subgrade, granular base, vapor retarder, concrete slab

questions.explanation: A slab-on-grade is the most economical floor for a building without a basement. The native soil is compacted after topsoil is removed, a granular base gives uniform support and breaks capillary rise, a polyethylene vapor retarder slows moisture moving up into the slab, and the concrete is commonly at least 4 in thick. In cold climates the edge is insulated.

questions.question_text: Why is footing reinforcement placed near the bottom of a footing, with 3 in of cover where concrete is cast against earth?

options.A: The footing bends like a simple beam, so the bottom is in compression, and cover keeps the soil from freezing
options.B: The footing bends like an upside-down cantilever, so the bottom is in tension, and cover protects the steel
options.C: The footing is loaded in tension by the column above, so the bars hold the column in place at the base
options.D: The footing is cracked by frost heave every winter, so the bars keep moisture out of the cracks

questions.explanation: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension. A footing loaded from above and pushed up by soil bends so that its bottom face is stretched, and bars are placed there. Spread footings usually contain a two-way grid, and light continuous footings often use a pair of continuous longitudinal bars for crack control. Cover protects steel from corrosion.

questions.question_text: Under what circumstances is a mat foundation chosen?

options.A: When soil is weak, column loads are heavy, or individual footings would nearly touch
options.B: When the soil is firm gravel and the building has only a few light columns to support
options.C: When the building has no floor, so a continuous footing under each wall is sufficient
options.D: When a basement is not allowed, so a thin slab replaces all of the footings

questions.explanation: A mat, or raft, is a thick continuous slab that spreads the whole building's load across its footprint. A common rule of thumb is that when footings would cover about half the building area, a mat becomes economical. It also resists differential settlement because the slab moves together, and it can sometimes replace both footings and floor slab, though it uses more concrete and steel.

questions.question_text: Which description fits a pile?

options.A: A hole drilled, fitted with a reinforcing cage, and filled with concrete, sometimes with a flared bell
options.B: A thick continuous slab that spreads a building's load over its whole footprint on weak soil
options.C: A long, slender column installed by driving or screwing it into the ground, such as a steel H-pile
options.D: A wide concrete pad under a single column, reaching below the frost depth to bear on firm soil

questions.explanation: Piles may be steel H-piles or pipe piles, precast concrete piles, or timber piles, and they are usually used in groups under a pile cap. Driving makes noise and vibration, so a quieter type may be chosen in a dense city. The drilled hole with a cage describes a drilled pier, the thick slab is a mat, and the pad under a column is a spread footing.

questions.question_text: A contractor must support heavy columns near occupied buildings where neighbors object to noise and vibration. Which choice and associated concern fit best?

options.A: Driven piles, which are quieter than drilling, but they are limited to very light columns and short spans
options.B: Drilled piers, which need no inspection because the concrete is placed under pressure and cannot be contaminated
options.C: Driven piles, which have a flared bell that increases end bearing but must be inspected open before placing concrete
options.D: Drilled piers, which can carry a heavy column quietly, but caving soil and water in the hole must be controlled

questions.explanation: A drilled pier is formed by drilling, placing a steel cage, and filling with concrete, and a bell at the base increases end-bearing area. Drilling is less noisy than driving, and one pier can carry a heavy column. The shafts must be inspected before concrete is placed because groundwater and caving soil can contaminate it. Driven piles are verified by blows per foot.

questions.question_text: Why is a vented crawl space often replaced by a sealed, conditioned one in cold climates?

options.A: Vents allow groundwater to enter the space, which raises hydrostatic pressure on the floor
options.B: Vents admit cold air that chills the floor and humid summer air that condenses on cool surfaces
options.C: Vents reduce the height of the space below the 18 in. minimum height required by the building code
options.D: Vents interfere with the insulation of the floor, which must be left uncovered so that air can pass

questions.explanation: A crawl space is a shallow unfinished space, usually 18 to 48 in high, beneath the first floor. Traditional vents let in cold air and moist summer air, causing the moisture and air-movement problems explained in Chapter 4. Modern practice is often to seal the space, cover the ground with heavy polyethylene, insulate the walls, and condition the space.

questions.question_text: A retaining wall is rebuilt at twice its original height with the same backfill. By what factor does the lateral force per foot of wall increase?
questions.explanation: The force on a retaining wall is F = ½ γ h², which grows with the square of the height, so doubling the height quadruples the force. A factor of 2 would apply to a linear relationship, 8 to a cube, and 16 to a fourth power. A retaining wall holds back soil at a change in ground level and has no floor to brace it at the top.

questions.question_text: Suppose the drainage fails and water fills the backfill behind an 8 ft basement wall designed for dry soil. What is the most important consequence?

options.A: Water alone adds about 499 psf at the base, more than the drained soil, so the wall can crack
options.B: The water lowers the lateral pressure because it carries part of the soil's weight on the wall
options.C: The water has no effect on the wall, since concrete is unaffected by moisture or by pressure
options.D: The water adds uplift on the roof framing, which must resist it with metal straps and hold-downs

questions.explanation: A perimeter drain, a perforated pipe in washed gravel wrapped in fabric, removes water before it can build pressure. Without it, water at 62.4 pcf gives about 499 psf at the base and about 1,997 lb per foot, which is already more than the 1,440 lb per foot from drained soil, and the soil still adds its own pressure. Drainage lowers the pressure and waterproofing resists what remains.

questions.question_text: In the Riverbend example, windows are 5 percent of the enclosure area but account for 36 percent of the conductive heat loss. What does this show?

options.A: Windows have the same U-value as walls, but they face the coldest direction of the building
options.B: The roof loses less heat than windows because it has a smaller temperature difference across it
options.C: Windows contribute to heat loss only through air leakage, which the table includes as conduction
options.D: A window loses about eight times as much heat per square foot as the wall, so window area matters

questions.explanation: Conductive loss equals U × A × ΔT. At a U-value of 0.30 versus 0.036 and the same 80°F design-day temperature difference, a window loses about 24 BTU/h per ft² against 2.9 for the wall, a ratio near 8 to 1. The roof is still the biggest single item because of its area, and the table does not include air leakage.

questions.question_text: In a cold-climate wall, which sequence of layers is correct from the outside in?

options.A: Interior finish, vapor control layer, cavity insulation, sheathing and air control layer, exterior insulation, water control layer, cladding
options.B: Cladding and drainage space, water control layer, exterior insulation, sheathing and air layer, cavity insulation, vapor layer, interior finish
options.C: Cladding, vapor control layer, exterior insulation, cavity insulation, sheathing and air control layer, water control layer, interior finish
options.D: Cladding, cavity insulation, sheathing and air control layer, water control layer, vapor control layer, interior finish

questions.explanation: Control layers must be continuous, in the right order for the climate, and may be served by one material doing more than one job. The water layer sits directly behind the cladding, and the vapor control layer sits near the warm interior face, where the wall is warm in winter. The first option reverses the order, and the others misplace the water or vapor layers.

questions.question_text: Why do cold-climate energy codes commonly pair cavity insulation with continuous insulation?

options.A: Cavity insulation alone loses much of its value to the framing, which acts as a thermal bridge
options.B: Cavity insulation cannot be installed in 2×6 walls, so exterior insulation is required
options.C: Continuous insulation is the only insulation that can act as a water control layer
options.D: Cavity insulation and continuous insulation must always be the same material to meet the code

questions.explanation: A wall assembly is the complete set of layers performing all four control functions along with structure and fire resistance. Performance belongs to the whole, not to any one product. Studs interrupt cavity insulation, so a combined wall has a higher effective R than the cavity alone.
