Walls are grouped as cavity-insulated, exterior-insulated, combined, or mass walls.

questions.question_text: A wall has a total R of 20 along the cavity path and 10 along the stud path, with framing occupying 25 percent of the area. What is the effective R-value using the parallel path method?
questions.explanation: The parallel path method averages U-values by area: U = 0.75 × (1/20) + 0.25 × (1/10) = 0.0375 + 0.025 = 0.0625, so R_eff = 1/0.0625 = 16.0. Averaging the R-values directly gives 17.5, which overstates the wall. The cavity R of 20 ignores the framing, and 30 adds the paths in series, which is wrong because they sit side by side.

questions.question_text: How does nearly all insulation resist the conduction of heat?

options.A: It reflects thermal radiation back into the room using a dense, highly polished metallic surface layer
options.B: It holds a large volume of still air or low-conductivity gas in a lightweight structure of fibers or cells
options.C: It stores heat in its mass and releases it slowly after the temperature on the other side drops
options.D: It blocks vapor diffusion entirely so the wall cavity stays at the indoor temperature all winter

questions.explanation: Air conducts heat poorly but moves easily by convection, so the material's structure must trap it. That is why insulation loses effectiveness when compressed, soaked, or full of gaps. Insulation comes as batts and loose fill, spray-applied foam, and rigid boards, and the R-value of a layer equals its R per inch times its thickness.

questions.question_text: A crew applies weather-resistive barrier courses from the top of the wall down, tucking each upper course behind the lower one. What is the result?

options.A: Water runs over the laps and continues down to the flashing, so the wall performs as designed
options.B: Water is trapped by the laps and evaporates through the siding without reaching the sheathing
options.C: Water runs behind the lower course onto the sheathing, turning the drainage plane into a funnel
options.D: Water is blocked completely because the double layer at each lap is thicker than a single layer

questions.explanation: The shingle principle laps every layer over the one below so water always flows over the top of the next piece, never behind it. A flipped lap uses identical materials and looks fine from the street, yet it directs water onto the sheathing. This is why inspectors check the laps before the cladding covers them.

questions.question_text: An enclosure leaks 500 cfm of air on a design day when the temperature difference is 60°F. Using Q = 1.08 × cfm × ΔT, how much heat is lost to leakage?

options.C: 540 BTU/h
options.D: 3,240 BTU/h

questions.explanation: Substituting gives 1.08 × 500 × 60 = 32,400 BTU/h. The constant 1.08 combines the density and specific heat of air and the 60 minutes in an hour. Omitting it gives 30,000, multiplying only the constant and the airflow gives 540, and 3,240 is a decimal slip. Leakage can exceed conduction through the whole enclosure, and it carries moisture into walls.

questions.question_text: Why is wall sheathing the surface most likely to become wet in a cold climate?

options.A: It sits on the warm side of the cavity insulation, where vapor condenses on its inner face
options.B: It is made of gypsum, which absorbs moisture from the humid indoor air and holds it for months
options.C: It is fastened with nails that conduct water through the cavity and onto the sheathing surface
options.D: It sits on the cold side of the cavity insulation, where leaking warm humid air meets a cold surface

questions.explanation: Sheathing is a rigid panel, often 7/16 in OSB, that serves as a structural skin, a substrate, a taped air control layer, and cavity closure. Wood-based sheathing tolerates occasional wetting but decays if it stays wet. Two defenses are used together: air and vapor control layers keep moisture from arriving, and continuous exterior insulation keeps the sheathing warmer so it dries.

questions.question_text: What property must a weather-resistive barrier have in addition to stopping liquid water?

options.A: It must be vapor permeable so that a wall that gets wet can dry outward
options.B: It must be a Class I vapor retarder so that no moisture reaches the sheathing
options.C: It must be rigid so that it can resist racking from wind and earthquakes
options.D: It must be thick enough to serve as the thermal control layer of the wall

questions.explanation: The WRB is the sheet or coating over the sheathing or exterior insulation that forms the water control layer behind the cladding. It must pass vapor, often called breathable. Codes commonly require laps of about 2 in horizontally and 6 in vertically, with flashing integrated at windows and doors. Types include building paper, housewrap, fluid-applied membranes, and self-adhered membranes.

questions.question_text: Many materials meet the code's air leakage limit, yet real buildings still leak. What explains this?

options.A: Air barrier materials lose their strength over time, so every material eventually fails the code limit
options.B: Air barriers work only when they are installed on the warm side of the wall, never on the cold side
options.C: An air barrier system is only as good as its seams and transitions, so the joints decide continuity
options.D: Air passes more easily through solid sheets than through cracks, so material choice does not matter

questions.explanation: An air barrier is a material that resists air passage, and the air barrier system joins such materials at their seams to form the air control layer. Every option in the chapter, such as taped OSB, sealed gypsum board, and lapped membranes, depends on its joints. Quality control on every seam, with surfaces clean and dry, matters as much as the material, and cracks leak far more than solid sheets.

questions.question_text: In the Riverbend example, 2 in of XPS (R-10) raised the effective R-value from 16.6 to 27.7, a gain of more than 10. What explains this?

options.A: The foam compresses the cavity insulation, so the cavity path gains extra resistance from the squeeze
options.B: The foam adds more R per inch than the studs lose, so the total is calculated by multiplying the two
options.C: The foam replaces the studs in the load path, so the stud path is no longer part of the average at all
options.D: The foam covers the studs as well as the cavities, so its R adds in full to every path and removes the bridge

questions.explanation: Continuous insulation is uninterrupted by framing, so it adds its R to both the cavity path and the stud path. Cavity path R goes to 32.4 and stud path R to 19.3, and the area-weighted U falls to 0.0361. Extra cavity insulation would have done nothing for the studs. The foam also keeps the sheathing about 23°F warmer, though air and vapor control layers are still needed.

questions.question_text: Why is it a mistake to put an impermeable vapor barrier on both sides of a Minnesota wall?

options.A: The two layers would double the rate at which vapor diffuses into the cavity
options.B: Any moisture that enters becomes trapped because the wall has no path to dry
options.C: The two layers would cancel each other so no vapor could reach the sheathing
options.D: The wall would lose its air control layer because impermeable layers cannot be sealed

questions.explanation: In winter, indoor vapor pressure is higher than outdoor pressure, so vapor diffuses outward and the control layer belongs on the warm interior side. The wall must be able to dry as well as resist wetting, so designers control vapor where it enters and leave a path for drying on the other side. Two impermeable layers trap whatever moisture gets in.

questions.question_text: How many inches of XPS board at about R-5 per inch are needed to add R-15 of continuous insulation?

options.A: 3 in
options.C: 10 in
options.D: 75 in

questions.explanation: The thickness needed equals the target R divided by the R per inch: 15 / 5 = 3 in. Dividing the other way gives 0.33, while 10 and 75 come from subtracting or multiplying. Rigid foam is EPS, XPS, or polyiso board that resists moisture and compression, and polyiso loses part of its R at low temperatures, which matters in Minnesota.

questions.question_text: How does waterproofing differ from dampproofing for a foundation wall?

options.A: Dampproofing is a continuous membrane that resists standing water, while waterproofing is only a thin asphalt coating
options.B: Dampproofing is applied on the inside of the wall, while waterproofing is applied on the outside face only
options.C: Dampproofing is a thin coating that resists soil moisture, while waterproofing is a membrane resisting hydrostatic pressure
options.D: Dampproofing is required only above grade, while waterproofing is required only at the footing and slab edge

questions.explanation: Dampproofing is an asphalt-based coating, commonly required on basement walls, that resists moisture in soil but not standing water. Waterproofing is a self-adhered or fluid-applied membrane typically required where the water table is high. It runs from the footing to above finished grade and is protected from backfill by a drainage board, and it works with the perimeter drain.

questions.question_text: How does a frost-protected foundation allow a footing to sit above the normal frost depth?

options.A: A layer of gravel beneath the footing drains away the water that would otherwise freeze under the footing in winter
options.B: Heat escaping from the building warms the soil, and rigid foam with a horizontal wing blocks cold from the footing
options.C: A thick concrete footing stores enough heat during the day to prevent freezing of the soil during the winter
options.D: A waterproofing membrane stops frost from penetrating the soil under the footing from the wall side and below

questions.explanation: The principle is that heat from a heated building keeps the soil beneath it warm, and insulation placed against the wall and extended outward prevents cold from reaching under the footing from the sides. Footings can be as shallow as 12 to 16 in. It is common for slab-on-grade houses and garages, but not suited to unheated buildings or poorly drained soil.

questions.question_text: Which classification and permeance fit a sheet of polyethylene used as a vapor retarder?

options.A: Class II, with a permeance above 0.1 perm up to 1 perm
options.B: Class III, with a permeance above 1 perm up to 10 perms
options.C: Class IV, with a permeance above 10 perms
options.D: Class I, with a permeance of 0.1 perm or less

questions.explanation: Codes sort vapor retarders into three classes by permeance. Class I, 0.1 perm or less, includes polyethylene sheet and sheet metal. Class II, up to 1.0 perm, includes kraft paper facing, and Class III, up to 10 perms, includes latex paint on gypsum board. A smart retarder changes permeance with humidity, closing in winter and opening in summer so the wall can dry.

questions.question_text: A crew folds fiberglass batts over wiring and compresses them to fit shallow cavities, and plans no separate air barrier. What problem does this create?

options.A: Folding raises the R-value, but the batts lose their fire resistance
options.B: Compression makes the batts waterproof, but the wall cannot dry
options.C: The batts become an air barrier, but they lose their ability to hold sound
options.D: Compression reduces the R-value, and the batts do not stop air movement

questions.explanation: Fiberglass is inexpensive and easy to install, but its performance depends on installation quality: fill the cavity fully, do not compress or fold the batt, and cut it to fit around wiring and boxes. It does not stop air movement, so it needs a separate air control layer. Insulation relies on trapped still air, so crushing it reduces its R-value.

questions.question_text: Why does mineral wool board suit exterior insulation where drying to the outside is desirable?

options.A: It repels liquid water but lets vapor pass, so a wall can dry outward, and it is noncombustible
options.B: It acts as a Class I vapor retarder, so no vapor can reach the sheathing from inside the building
options.C: It has the highest R per inch of any insulation, so much thinner layers are needed for the same R
options.D: It is lightweight and inexpensive, so it is the cheapest choice for continuous insulation

questions.explanation: Mineral wool is made from spun basalt rock or industrial slag. It is noncombustible, commonly used in fire-rated assemblies, and its density makes it a good sound absorber. Its vapor permeability gives it an advantage over foam plastics in exterior applications. It is heavier and more expensive than fiberglass, with R per inch similar to or slightly higher.

questions.question_text: Why is cellulose often dense-packed in closed wall cavities?

options.A: Dense-packing converts cellulose into an air barrier, so no other air control layer is needed anywhere
options.B: Dense-packing makes cellulose waterproof, so it can be installed on the cold side of the sheathing
options.C: Dense-packing fills voids around wiring and framing better than batts and slows air movement in the cavity
options.D: Dense-packing eliminates settling, so the labeled R-value is guaranteed without any added depth in the attic

questions.explanation: Cellulose is made mostly from recycled newsprint treated with borate compounds that resist fire, insects, and mold. Blown at a higher density it fills irregular spaces that batts cannot, though it is not a substitute for an air barrier. It absorbs and releases moisture, which buffers short wetting events, but it must be kept dry, and loose-fill depth settles over time.

questions.question_text: Why might closed-cell spray foam be chosen for a rim joist in a Minnesota house?

options.A: It is vapor-permeable and soft, so it lets the rim joist dry in both directions
options.B: It seals air leaks and insulates in one step, with the highest R per inch of the foams
options.C: It is the lowest cost per R of any insulation, so large areas can be covered economically
options.D: It is noncombustible and so needs no thermal barrier where it is exposed

questions.explanation: Both types of spray foam seal air leaks as they cure, so one application can supply the thermal and air control layers. Closed-cell foam is denser, has about R-6 to R-7 per inch, stiffens the surface, and in a few inches acts as a Class II vapor retarder. Open-cell is soft, about R-3.6 per inch, and vapor-permeable. Closed-cell costs much more per R and must be installed by trained crews.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why is cladding described as the first line of defense and not as the water control layer?

options.A: It is applied last in the sequence, so it is installed only after the water control layer is no longer needed
options.B: It sheds most rain and snow, but some water gets behind it, where the weather-resistive barrier acts as the second line
options.C: It is face-sealed in every cladding system, so water that gets past the surface cannot reach the layers behind
options.D: It is the only layer that must be continuous, so the barrier behind it may have gaps without consequence

questions.explanation: Cladding is the exterior skin that sheds water, protects the layers behind from sunlight, impact, and wear, gives the building its appearance, and contributes to fire performance. Most modern walls use a drained strategy that assumes some water will get behind it and provides a path out. A face-sealed system tries to keep all water out, so every joint must stay watertight for the wall's life.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: A joint must accommodate 0.30 in. of thermal movement, and the sealant is rated for plus or minus 25 percent. What is the minimum joint width?
questions.explanation: The minimum width equals the movement divided by twice the movement capability: 0.30 / (2 × 0.25) = 0.6 in. Using the movement alone ignores the sealant's capability, 1.2 in. doubles the result, and 0.15 in. uses a rating of 100 percent. A narrow 1/8 in. joint would tear on the first cold night, and sealant should adhere on two sides only, with a backer rod behind it.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Which type of glass is heat-treated to be about four times stronger and breaks into small, blunt pieces?

options.A: Annealed glass
options.B: Laminated glass
options.C: Insulating glass
options.D: Tempered glass

questions.explanation: Tempered glass is heat-treated for strength and safety. Annealed glass is ordinary, slowly cooled glass that breaks into sharp shards, and laminated glass has a plastic layer between two panes that holds pieces together and improves sound reduction and security. An insulating glass unit is two or three panes separated by a sealed gap, not a strength treatment. Codes require safety glazing where people are likely to strike glass.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why is air sealing done before the drywall is installed?

options.A: The air barrier material is installed only on the outside of the wall, so the drywall would block it
options.B: The drywall must be sealed with spray foam on both faces, which requires the framing to be open
options.C: Most leakage occurs at joints and penetrations, and open framing lets the crew reach every one cheaply
options.D: Building codes require an inspection of the framing before drywall regardless of air leakage

questions.explanation: A wall can have a perfect air barrier material and still leak at the top plate, rim joist, window and door gaps, penetrations, and electrical boxes. Sealants, gaskets, tape, and foam close them. Leaks hidden behind finished drywall are expensive to find and repair, and nearly impossible to do well afterward. Low-expansion foam is used around windows to avoid bowing the frame.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: On a design day, indoor air is 70°F and outdoor air is −10°F. A window with U-0.55 has an inside film resistance of 0.68. The room's dew point is 45°F. What happens at the glass?

options.A: The inside surface is about 26°F, but condensation does not occur because the glass is dry
options.B: The inside surface is about 54°F, above the dew point, so the glass stays clear
options.C: The inside surface is about 40°F, below the dew point, so moisture condenses
options.D: The inside surface is about 70°F, equal to the room air, so no heat flows

questions.explanation: The surface temperature is T_in − U × ΔT × 0.68 = 70 − 0.55 × 80 × 0.68 ≈ 40°F, below the 45°F dew point, so moisture condenses and may freeze. Leaving out the film resistance gives about 26°F, and a low-U window such as U-0.28 would stay near 55°F. The glass edge is colder than the center, so real condensation starts earlier.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: A blower door holds 50 Pa at 4,500 CFM50 in a building of 90,000 ft³. What is the ACH50?
questions.explanation: ACH50 = CFM50 × 60 / volume = 4,500 × 60 / 90,000 = 3.0. Forgetting the factor of 60 gives 0.05, and 30 and 1.5 are order-of-magnitude and halving errors. A calibrated fan depressurizes the building by 50 pascals, and natural leakage is commonly estimated by dividing ACH50 by 15 to 20. Cold-climate residential codes commonly require about 3 ACH50 or less.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: What distinguishes Type X gypsum board?

options.A: Its core has added glass fibers that help it hold together in a fire, so it builds rated assemblies
options.B: Its core has added moisture-resistant additives, so it can be used in showers and other wet areas
options.C: Its paper facing is replaced with foil, so it also acts as both a vapor barrier and an air barrier
options.D: Its thickness is limited to 1/4 in., so it is used only as a covering over existing walls and ceilings

questions.explanation: Gypsum board has a core of gypsum, a mineral that holds water chemically, pressed between sheets of heavy paper. Type X is used to build the fire-resistance-rated assemblies described in Chapter 18. Moisture-resistant types serve wet areas, and plain paper-faced board should be kept dry because wet paper supports mold. Panels are commonly 1/2 or 5/8 in. thick.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: What is the function of weep holes in a brick veneer wall?

options.A: They hold the brick to the backup wall to resist wind pressure on the wall
options.B: They let water collected on the flashing drain out of the cavity
options.C: They support the brick above windows and doors at the top of each opening
options.D: They allow air to circulate in the cavity so the brick can expand freely

questions.explanation: A brick veneer wall has an air space, metal ties, flashing, weep holes, and lintels. Flashing at the base and above openings catches water running down the cavity, and weep holes in the mortar joints just above the flashing let it out. Ties hold the brick to the backup, and steel angle lintels hold the brick above openings. Veneer carries only its own weight.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why are vinyl siding nail holes slotted and the nails not driven tight?

options.A: Vinyl is soft, so tight nails would crush it during installation
options.B: Vinyl is a drainage layer, so tight nails would block water paths
options.C: Vinyl is combustible, so loose nails reduce the spread of fire
options.D: Vinyl expands and contracts with temperature, so it needs room to move

questions.explanation: Siding is a family of thin, lapped cladding boards or panels fastened in courses, with each course overlapping the one below to shed water by the shingle principle. Vinyl moves with temperature, so the nails must allow it to slide. Fiber cement resists rot and fire, but cutting it creates silica dust that can harm lungs, so dust control is required.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: In a traditional three-coat stucco system, what is the correct order of the coats?

options.A: Brown coat, scratch coat, finish coat
options.B: Scratch coat, brown coat, finish coat
options.C: Finish coat, brown coat, scratch coat
options.D: Scratch coat, finish coat, brown coat

questions.explanation: Stucco is a cement-based plaster applied in layers over lath. The scratch coat is pressed into the lath and scored for grip, the brown coat levels and builds thickness, and the finish coat provides the colored or textured surface. Stucco is hard and fire-resistant but cracks as the building moves, so over wood framing it needs a water-resistive barrier and often a drainage mat.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Which two design problems must be addressed in a metal panel wall because of the properties of metal?

options.A: Thermal bridging at clips and girts, and movement of panels with temperature changes at the joints
options.B: Moisture absorption in the panels, and rot of the supporting framing behind the panels over time
options.C: Combustibility of the panels, and shrinkage of the panels as they dry out after installation
options.D: Low strength of the panels, and galvanic corrosion caused by contact with the wood framing

questions.explanation: Metal panels are light, durable, and common on commercial and industrial buildings. Because metal conducts heat well, the clips and girts create thermal bridges unless thermal breaks are used, and because it moves with temperature, the joints must be sized for that movement, as in the sealant calculation. Panels are normally installed as a rainscreen, with an air space behind them.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Which three benefits does the gap in a rainscreen provide?

options.A: Insulation, air sealing, and vapor control
options.B: Fire resistance, sound reduction, and structural support
options.C: Drainage, drying by moving air, and a capillary break
options.D: Weight reduction, cost savings, and faster installation

questions.explanation: A rainscreen has a gap, often 3/4 in. or more, between the cladding and the water-resistive barrier. Water that gets past the cladding falls down the gap, moving air dries the wall, and the gap stops capillary action. A pressure-equalized rainscreen also matches the gap pressure to wind pressure outside so wind has less force pushing rain through joints. Riverbend mounts siding on vertical furring strips to form the gap.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why can a curtain wall be thin and highly glazed?

options.A: It is a load-bearing wall made of glass panels, and the glass carries the floor loads in compression
options.B: It is attached to the foundation, and the foundation carries the wind load directly into the ground
options.C: It is made of aluminum, which is strong enough to replace the structural frame of the building
options.D: It hangs from the structure and carries only its own weight and wind, since the structure carries the floors

questions.explanation: A curtain wall is typically an aluminum frame with glass or panels as infill, and it is the usual exterior of a multi-story commercial building. Because it is a complete enclosure, its frame must include water, air, vapor, and thermal control layers, and it needs thermal breaks, strips of low-conductivity plastic, because bare aluminum conducts heat very well. A storefront is the one-story version.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: At the head of a window opening, how should the weather-resistive barrier be installed relative to the head flashing?

options.A: Tucked under the head flashing, so the barrier is protected from the sun and from impact
options.B: Lapped over the head flashing, so water on the barrier runs onto the flashing and outward
options.C: Omitted above the flashing, so the sheathing can dry upward through the opening toward the attic
options.D: Replaced with a bead of caulk across the top of the window, which seals the joint

questions.explanation: Flashing directs water out of the wall. The top of the flashing tucks behind the weather-resistive barrier, and the bottom laps over the cladding below, which is the shingle principle. If the barrier were under the head flashing, water would flow behind the flashing and into the opening. Caulk is only a backup, because sealant ages, cracks, and leaves a gap.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why do designers commonly place a low-E coating on surface 3 in a heating climate and on surface 2 in a cooling climate?

options.A: Surface 3 reflects visible light into the room, and surface 2 absorbs visible light from outdoors
options.B: Surface 3 protects the coating from the weather, and surface 2 exposes it for easier cleaning
options.C: Surface 3 keeps heat in the room while admitting solar heat, and surface 2 rejects more solar heat
options.D: Surface 3 reduces the glass's emissivity to zero, and surface 2 increases the glass's emissivity

questions.explanation: A low-E coating is a microscopically thin metal or metal-oxide layer that reflects long-wave infrared radiation, or heat, while passing visible light, lowering emissivity from about 0.84 to roughly 0.04 to 0.20. It is placed inside the sealed unit where it is protected. It can lower the U-factor of a double pane by about a third.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Two windows with a combined 100 ft² of glazing have whole-window U-factors of 0.48 and 0.28. On a design day with an 80°F temperature difference, how much more heat does the 0.48 option lose?

options.A: 1,600 BTU/h
options.B: 2,240 BTU/h
options.C: 3,840 BTU/h
options.D: 640 BTU/h

questions.explanation: Heat flow is U × A × ΔT. The 0.48 window loses 0.48 × 100 × 80 = 3,840 BTU/h and the 0.28 window loses 2,240 BTU/h, so the difference is 1,600 BTU/h. The other values are the individual losses or a slip. The NFRC label reports the whole-window value, which is higher than center-of-glass because the frame and edge conduct more heat.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: What does the solar heat gain coefficient measure?

options.A: The rate of heat flow through the whole window per square foot per degree of temperature difference
options.B: The percentage of visible light that passes through the glass and the frame into the room
options.C: The fraction of the sun's energy striking a window that passes through as heat, from 0 to 1
options.D: The fraction of long-wave infrared radiation that the coating reflects back into the room

questions.explanation: SHGC helps predict solar gain: heat gained equals SHGC × glass area × solar irradiance. A low SHGC reduces cooling loads and glare, while a high SHGC helps heat a building in winter, so Minneapolis designers commonly use a high SHGC on the south side and a low one where sun would cause overheating. The heat-flow rate is the U-factor, and visible light is visible transmittance.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why do busy building entries often include a vestibule with two sets of doors?

options.A: Doors opened by many people cause the largest bursts of air leakage, and two sets keep one closed
options.B: Doors need two sets so that the sill pan can be sloped outward on both sides of the vestibule
options.C: Egress codes require two doors in series so that occupants can exit the building in two steps
options.D: Two sets of doors provide a thermal bridge that helps warm the entry during the winter months

questions.explanation: An exterior door is a slab, a frame, a threshold, and weatherstripping, and it is another hole in the control layers. Water enters under the threshold, so it needs a sill pan and sloped threshold, and air leaks around the perimeter, so it needs weatherstripping and a sweep. A thermal break in the frame and threshold avoids thermal bridging. An egress door typically needs a clear opening of at least 32 in. wide.

questions.chapter: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
questions.question_text: Why should flooring and paint be installed only after the building is enclosed and the slab is dry?

options.A: They are the first layer of the air barrier, so they must be completed before the drywall is hung
options.B: They are required to pass the blower door test, so they must be finished before the test begins
options.C: They cure by absorbing moisture from the slab, so a wet building improves their bond to the floor
options.D: They are damaged by moisture, and finishes are the last materials installed in the construction sequence

questions.explanation: Interior finishes are surface materials such as paint, tile, flooring, ceilings, and wall base, selected for durability, cleaning, appearance, acoustics, and fire behavior. Codes assign flame-spread classes A, B, or C and limit the class allowed in corridors, exits, and assembly rooms. Low-emitting products reduce chemicals in indoor air. They are not part of the air barrier and are installed after air sealing and inspections.

questions.question_text: Why does a ventilated-attic roof place the air barrier at the ceiling plane and not at the roof covering?

options.A: Air leaking upward through ceiling penetrations carries moisture into the attic, so air must be stopped there
options.B: The covering must be left open so that the roof deck can absorb moisture from the shingles above it
options.C: The ceiling is the coldest layer in the roof, so the barrier belongs there to prevent condensation on drywall
options.D: The shingles act as the vapor retarder, so the barrier is placed at the ceiling to avoid any duplication

questions.explanation: A roof assembly is the full stack of materials from deck to weathering surface, and leaks almost always trace to joints between layers. In the example, the insulation controls heat and the covering controls only water. Moisture in leaking air is the reason the ceiling air barrier is critical, and the attic stays near outdoor temperature because it is ventilated.

questions.question_text: A 6:12 roof covers a building footprint of 1,000 ft². Using the slope factor of about 1.12, what is the sloped roof area before waste?

options.A: About 1,000 ft²
options.B: About 1,030 ft²
options.C: About 1,410 ft²
options.D: About 1,120 ft²

questions.explanation: A steep-slope roof is pitched so water runs off by gravity over overlapping layers, and slope is stated as rise per 12 in. of run. For 6:12 the slope factor is √(12² + 6²)/12 ≈ 1.12, so the area is 1,120 ft². Using the footprint alone undercounts material, 1.03 is the factor for 3:12, and 1.41 is the factor for 12:12. Roofers then add about 10 percent for waste.

questions.question_text: A low-slope roof is not flat. Why do designers slope it, often with tapered insulation?

options.A: A slope lets water run off over overlapping units, as it does on a conventional shingled roof surface
options.B: A slope allows the membrane to be omitted, because gravity removes the water before it can enter
options.C: A slope of at least one-quarter inch per foot moves water to drains so it does not stand on the membrane
options.D: A slope reduces the thickness of insulation needed over the whole roof, so the roof costs less

questions.explanation: Low-slope roofs rely on a continuous waterproof membrane and are common on commercial, institutional, and industrial buildings. The slope often comes from tapered insulation, boards cut with a slope, so a structurally level deck can still drain. Over a 30 ft run to a drain, a quarter-inch-per-foot slope changes thickness by 7.5 in., a quantity that must be carried into parapet details.

questions.question_text: Why do codes commonly require a secondary overflow drain on a low-slope roof with a parapet?

options.A: The primary drains are too small for any rainfall, so the secondary drain handles all normal storms alone
options.B: If primary drains clog, ponding adds load, the deck deflects, and the dip holds more water, risking collapse
options.C: Standing water on the roof improves insulation, so the overflow limits how much benefit it provides in winter
options.D: Parapets prevent water from leaving the roof, so the overflow replaces the primary drains during the winter

questions.explanation: Water weighs about 5.2 psf per inch of depth, so 2 in. of ponding adds about 10.4 psf, roughly 94,000 lb over a 9,000 ft² roof. A secondary drain or scupper set slightly higher acts as the safety valve. Structural engineers also check roofs for rain load. The overflow is a backup, not the normal path, and standing water offers no useful insulation.

questions.question_text: A roof sits over a restaurant kitchen and is exposed to grease and chemicals. Which membrane family fits best, and why?

options.A: EPDM, which is a rubber sheet that dissolves in contact with grease
options.B: Built-up roofing, which is held down by stone ballast that absorbs grease
options.C: PVC, which is heat-welded and offers good chemical resistance
options.D: Modified bitumen, which is applied only by mechanical fasteners and cannot resist chemicals

questions.explanation: A roofing membrane is a continuous, flexible, waterproof sheet or built-up layer that forms the weathering surface of a low-slope roof. EPDM is synthetic rubber with taped seams, TPO is a heat-welded single ply, PVC is heat-welded with chemical resistance, modified bitumen is polymer-reinforced asphalt, and BUR alternates felts and hot bitumen. Most failures occur at seams, penetrations, and edges.

questions.question_text: An attic has 1,500 ft² of floor area, a ceiling vapor retarder, and vents split between high and low. At the 1:300 ratio, what total net free vent area is required?

options.A: 720 in²
options.B: 360 in²
options.C: 5 in²

questions.explanation: At 1:300, the net free area is 1,500 / 300 = 5 ft², which is 5 × 144 = 720 in², split about half at the soffit and half at the ridge. The value 360 in² is only the soffit half, 5 forgets the unit conversion, and 1,440 uses the 1:150 ratio, which applies when the conditions for the lower ratio are not met. Baffles keep an air path open above the insulation.

questions.question_text: Which statement about shingles is correct?

options.A: They form a continuous waterproof surface, so the underlayment beneath them is optional on any roof slope
options.B: They are laid from the ridge downward so each course sheds water over the joint above it on the roof
options.C: They are made of metal panels that run from ridge to eave and are held by concealed clips on the deck
options.D: They shed water over overlapping courses and rely on underlayment and flashing, and most leaks start at flashing

questions.explanation: Shingles are small overlapping units laid in courses from the eave upward. Asphalt shingles are a fiberglass mat saturated with asphalt and topped with mineral granules, and they commonly last about 20 to 30 years. A cold-climate system includes a drip edge, self-adhering underlayment at the eaves, underlayment over the deck, and flashing at valleys, chimneys, walls, and penetrations.

questions.question_text: Why must metal roof panels be free to slide on their clips, and why do designers add snow guards?

options.A: Metal absorbs moisture and swells, and snow guards keep the panels from corroding when snow melts
options.B: Metal expands and contracts with temperature, and snow can slide off a smooth roof suddenly above walkways
options.C: Metal conducts lightning strikes, and snow guards ground the roof to protect the occupants below
options.D: Metal is soft and bends under load, and snow guards support the panels against the weight of snow

questions.explanation: A 20 ft steel panel with a 100°F swing changes length by about 0.16 in., and aluminum by about twice as much. Standing seam systems use concealed clips that let panels move and avoid fasteners that loosen and leak, while exposed-fastener panels use screws with sealing washers. Metal roofs commonly last 40 years or more and shed snow readily, which is why snow guards are used.

questions.question_text: Why do air sealing and insulation come before ventilation and heating cables when preventing ice dams?

options.A: Ice dams are caused by cold air entering the attic, so ventilation addresses the cause only last
options.B: Ice dams are caused by shingles that are too thin, so extra insulation thickens the roof covering
options.C: Ice dams are caused by heat escaping from the house, so remedies must first stop the heat source
options.D: Ice dams are caused by rain falling on the eave, so the ice barrier should be installed first

questions.explanation: Heat warms the deck above freezing, snow melts from beneath, and the meltwater refreezes at the cold overhanging eave and builds a dam that backs water up under the shingles. Ventilation only dilutes heat that has already escaped. A self-adhering ice-and-water barrier is a backup that protects the interior but does not stop the dam, and heating cables do nothing about the heat loss.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes an extensive green roof from an intensive one?

options.A: An extensive roof replaces the waterproofing membrane, while an intensive roof sits above the membrane
options.B: An extensive roof uses a thin growing medium of 3 to 6 in. with hardy plants, while an intensive roof uses deeper soil
options.C: An extensive roof supports small trees and walkable gardens, while an intensive roof supports only hardy sedums
options.D: An extensive roof needs constant irrigation and weighs more, while an intensive roof needs none and is lighter

questions.explanation: A green roof is a roof assembly topped with vegetation in a lightweight growing medium, with filter fabric, a drainage layer, a root barrier, the waterproofing membrane, insulation, and the deck beneath. The green layer sits above the membrane and protects it. A 4 in. medium at 90 pcf adds about 30 psf, so the structure must be designed for it from the start.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: A room has a heating load of 12,000 BTU/h, and supply air at 100°F serves a room held at 70°F. Using Q = 1.08 × cfm × ΔT, what airflow is needed?

options.A: About 400 cfm
options.B: About 370 cfm
options.C: About 12,960 cfm
options.D: About 33 cfm

questions.explanation: The temperature difference is 30°F, so cfm = 12,000 / (1.08 × 30) ≈ 370. Omitting the 1.08 constant, which combines air density, minutes per hour, and specific heat, gives 400. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 12,960. HVAC maintains temperature, humidity, and air quality, and it is a response to the building, since the enclosure sets the load.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why can supply pipes run in any direction while drain pipes must slope continuously downhill?

options.A: Supply pipes are larger than drain pipes, so they can carry water uphill by capillary action and suction
options.B: Drain pipes are sealed and pressurized, while supply pipes are open to the atmosphere through vents on the roof
options.C: Supply pipes carry only cold water, while drain pipes carry only hot water from the fixtures to the sewer
options.D: Supply pipes are sealed and pressurized, while drain pipes are partly full, vented to the atmosphere, and drain by gravity

questions.explanation: Plumbing is really three systems: the pressurized water supply, the gravity drain-waste-vent system, and the stormwater system. This difference explains why a drain often controls the layout of a floor. A flush sends waste through a trap, a branch drain, a stack, a building drain, and the building sewer, with the vent supplying air behind the flowing water.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Which pair correctly distinguishes passive from active fire protection?

options.A: Passive features such as sprinklers respond to a fire, while active features such as rated walls divide the building
options.B: Passive features such as alarms warn occupants, while active features such as rated floors suppress the fire
options.C: Passive features such as rated walls work without moving parts, while active features such as sprinklers respond to a fire
options.D: Passive features operate only in winter when heating is on, while active features operate only in summer

questions.explanation: Fire protection combines features that prevent a fire from starting, detect it, alert occupants, limit spread, and control or extinguish it. The chain of five jobs is detect, warn, suppress, control smoke, and contain. A building usually relies on several at once, because any single system can fail. Rated walls, floors, and doors compartmentalize and slow the spread, which is the passive part.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: A classroom has 20 occupants and 800 ft² of floor area. Using 10 cfm per person plus 0.12 cfm per ft², what outdoor airflow is required?

options.A: 296 cfm
options.B: 200 cfm
options.C: 96 cfm

questions.explanation: Required outdoor airflow is the people rate plus the area rate: 10 × 20 + 0.12 × 800 = 200 + 96 = 296 cfm. The value 200 counts only people and 96 counts only floor area. Standards such as ASHRAE 62.1 combine both because contaminants come from people and from the building itself. Heating this much outdoor air in winter can exceed the conduction load.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why can a heat pump with a COP of 3 deliver more heat energy than the electrical energy it uses?

options.A: It burns fuel more efficiently than a furnace, so each unit of electricity makes three units of heat
options.B: It stores heat in its refrigerant during the night, so daytime use is lower
options.C: It uses a higher voltage than resistance heaters, so the energy is multiplied
options.D: It moves heat that already exists instead of creating it by combustion or resistance

questions.explanation: Combustion equipment is rated by AFUE, the fraction of fuel energy that becomes useful heat over a season. A heat pump is rated by COP, the ratio of heat delivered to electrical energy used, and the figure exceeds 1 because heat is moved from a cooler place to a warmer one. COP falls as outdoor temperature falls, so cold-climate models and sizing matter in Minnesota.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Street pressure is 55 psi, the meter and backflow preventer use 8 psi, and a fixture sits 30 ft above the service entrance. Water produces 0.433 psi per foot of height. What pressure reaches the fixture?

options.A: About 47 psi
options.B: About 17 psi
options.C: About 34 psi
options.D: About 55 psi

questions.explanation: Lift costs 30 × 0.433 ≈ 13 psi, so the pressure at the fixture is 55 − 8 − 13 ≈ 34 psi. The value 47 forgets the lift, 17 subtracts the pressure twice, and 55 ignores all losses. If pressure is too low, a booster pump is needed, so designers request available street pressure before sizing pipes. Codes commonly limit static pressure to about 80 psi, and backflow preventers protect the public system.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: How do most cooling systems remove heat from indoor air and reject it outdoors?

options.A: A heat exchanger that passes cold outdoor air directly across the indoor coil to cool the supply air
options.B: A refrigeration cycle where the evaporator absorbs heat and the condenser rejects it outdoors
options.C: A boiler that cools water by circulating it through radiant floor loops and then through the chiller
options.D: A furnace that reverses its blower to pull heat out of the rooms and discharge it through the flue

questions.explanation: Nearly all cooling uses the same refrigeration cycle as a heat pump: the evaporator sits in the airstream or a water loop and absorbs heat, and the compressor and condenser reject it outdoors. Chillers cool water that is piped to coils in larger buildings, and evaporative cooling works best in dry climates. Cooling matters in Minnesota where occupancy, glass, or equipment adds heat.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why is a balanced system, often with a heat recovery ventilator, preferred for tight cold-climate buildings over exhaust-only or supply-only?

options.A: Exhaust-only draws replacement air through the envelope, supply-only pushes warm moist air into walls, and balanced matches flows
options.B: Exhaust-only provides too much outdoor air, and supply-only provides too little, so only balanced meets any code requirement
options.C: Exhaust-only cannot be controlled by sensors, and supply-only cannot filter air, so only a balanced system can do both
options.D: Exhaust-only and supply-only systems are illegal in Minnesota, so only balanced systems are approved by officials

questions.explanation: In a tight building, air sealing leaves too little leakage to ventilate. An exhaust-only system pulls air out through fans and lets replacement air leak in, which can draw radon or combustion gases through the envelope. A supply-only system pressurizes the building and pushes humid air into walls in winter. A balanced system uses equal flows, and commercial buildings often add demand-controlled ventilation using CO₂ sensors.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a vent in a drain-waste-vent system?

options.A: It admits air so that water flows freely and traps keep their seals
options.B: It carries solids away from the fixture by gravity to the building drain
options.C: It supplies pressurized hot water to the fixture from the water heater
options.D: It holds a plug of water that blocks sewer gas from entering the room

questions.explanation: The DWV system is gravity piping that removes used water and sewage and admits air through vents that terminate above the roof. Without a vent, flowing water would pull a trap dry, and sewer gas would enter the room. The trap is the part that holds water. Small horizontal drains commonly slope about one-quarter inch per foot, and cleanouts allow a clogged pipe to be rodded.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: A branch duct must carry 400 cfm at a design velocity of 800 feet per minute. What cross-sectional area is required?

options.A: 36 in²
options.B: 0.5 in²
options.C: 72 in²
options.D: 5 in²

questions.explanation: Airflow equals velocity times area, so area = 400 / 800 = 0.5 ft², which is 72 in². The value 36 in² uses 72 divided by two, and 0.5 forgets to convert from square feet. A duct that is too small makes air move too fast, which causes noise and uses fan energy. Ducts compete with beams for ceiling space, a typical source of design conflict.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: How does an energy recovery ventilator (ERV) differ from a heat recovery ventilator (HRV)?

options.A: An HRV mixes the exhaust and incoming air streams, while an ERV keeps the two streams completely separate
options.B: Both pass exhaust and incoming air through a heat exchanger without mixing, but an ERV also transfers moisture
options.C: An HRV transfers moisture between the streams, while an ERV transfers only heat between them
options.D: An HRV is used only in houses, while an ERV is used only in large commercial buildings

questions.explanation: An HRV preheats incoming fresh air using the outgoing exhaust air, without mixing the two. With 75 percent sensible effectiveness, 0°F outdoor air is warmed to about 52.5°F, recovering about 18,300 of the 24,300 BTU/h needed in the classroom example. An ERV adds moisture transfer. In a cold climate, recovery is usually the main reason to install the device.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: In what order are the three strategies for controlling indoor air quality applied?

options.A: Filter the air first, ventilate to dilute what remains, and then remove the source of the contaminants
options.B: Ventilate to dilute the contaminants, filter the air, and then redesign the building enclosure entirely
options.C: Test for contaminants, filter the air, and then ventilate only if the test results show a problem
options.D: Remove or avoid the source, ventilate to dilute what remains, then filter to capture particles

questions.explanation: IAQ is the condition of the air inside a building as it affects health and comfort. Contaminants include carbon dioxide, VOCs from paints and adhesives, particles, combustion gases, moisture and mold, and radon. Source control comes first because it is most effective, filters are rated by MERV, and carbon dioxide level is only a rough indicator of ventilation quality.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: What do federal standards limit for common toilets and showerheads?

options.A: About 5 gallons per flush for toilets and about 10 gallons per minute for showerheads
options.B: About 0.5 gallons per flush for toilets and about 1 gallon per minute for showerheads
options.C: About 1.6 gallons per flush for toilets and about 2.5 gallons per minute for showerheads
options.D: About 3 gallons per flush for toilets and about 5 gallons per minute for showerheads

questions.explanation: A plumbing fixture receives water from the supply system and discharges used water to the drain system, and every fixture has a trap, a drain, and a vent. Codes set a minimum number of fixtures by occupancy, so Riverbend's multipurpose room requires more toilets than a small office. Efficient fixtures lower both water and water-heating energy, and accessibility rules govern mounting heights and clearances.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why does sub-slab depressurization keep radon out of a building?

options.A: A membrane under the slab absorbs the radon and converts it to harmless carbon dioxide in the soil
options.B: A fan draws soil gas from a gravel layer under the slab and discharges it above the roof
options.C: A filter at the furnace removes radon from the indoor air before it is breathed by the occupants
options.D: A vent at the foundation wall pushes soil gas into the basement so it can be diluted by room air

questions.explanation: Radon is a radioactive gas released from soil that seeps through cracks because air pressure in a heated building is usually lower than in the soil. Long-term exposure raises lung cancer risk, and much of Minnesota has high radon potential. Sealing cracks and testing after construction complete the strategy, and some codes require the piping to be roughed in for new houses.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: What distinguishes a condensing furnace from a standard furnace?

options.A: It burns no fuel at all, so it needs no vent and heats the air using resistance heating elements
options.B: It heats water for hydronic distribution through pipes instead of heating air for distribution in ducts
options.C: It uses a refrigeration cycle to move heat from the outdoor air into the building, rather than burning fuel
options.D: It extracts so much heat that exhaust gases condense, so it vents through plastic pipe and drains condensate

questions.explanation: A furnace burns gas, propane, or oil, passes the hot gases through a heat exchanger, and uses a blower to push household air over it, so combustion gases never mix with room air. Condensing models reach very high AFUE. Because combustion produces carbon monoxide, furnaces require a proper vent and combustion air, and CO alarms are commonly required near sleeping areas. Electric furnaces need no vent.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why do hydronic systems use small pipes where an air system would need large ducts?

options.A: Water holds far more heat per volume than air, so small pipes carry the same amount of heat
options.B: Water flows much faster than air through any pipe, so the pipes can be smaller than the ducts
options.C: Boilers produce only steam, so pressure forces the water through small pipes at high velocity
options.D: Pipes are better insulated than ducts, so they lose less heat in transit through the building

questions.explanation: A boiler heats water, or steam in older systems, and sends it to radiators, baseboards, and radiant floor loops. It allows zoning with pumps and valves and is common in schools, hospitals, and apartment buildings. Condensing boilers reach their best efficiency when return water is cool, which suits low-temperature radiant systems. Gas boilers still need venting and combustion air.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: To deliver the same heat, how much electricity does a heat pump operating at COP 3 draw compared with electric resistance heating?

options.A: About the same
options.B: About three times as much
options.C: About one-third as much
options.D: About one-half as much

questions.explanation: Electric resistance converts each kilowatt of electricity into one kilowatt of heat, while a heat pump at COP 3 delivers three units of heat for each unit of electricity. To deliver 23.4 kW of heat, resistance draws 23.4 kW and the heat pump draws 7.8 kW. COP falls with outdoor temperature, so at a COP of 2 it draws about half as much as resistance.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: What is the difference between latent cooling and sensible cooling?

options.A: Latent cooling lowers air temperature, while sensible cooling removes moisture by condensation
options.B: Latent cooling removes moisture by condensing vapor on a cold coil, while sensible cooling lowers air temperature
options.C: Latent cooling is done by evaporative cooling only, while sensible cooling uses a chiller only
options.D: Latent cooling rejects heat outdoors, while sensible cooling stores the heat in the building mass

questions.explanation: Air conditioning treats air to control temperature, humidity, cleanliness, and distribution at once. Cooling air below its dew point makes water vapor condense on the cold coil, which dehumidifies the air. This matters because the body feels warmer in humid air. An oversized unit cools quickly, shuts off, and never runs long enough to remove humidity.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: A bedroom's door is closed, and the room has no return opening or transfer grille. What is the likely result?

options.A: The room becomes depressurized and draws in more air from the other rooms, which improves overall comfort
options.B: The room's diffuser throws air farther along the ceiling, which improves mixing and reduces drafts
options.C: The room's supply air bypasses the equipment entirely, so the furnace shuts down on a safety limit
options.D: The room becomes pressurized and starves other rooms of air, since air must flow out as fast as it flows in

questions.explanation: Air distribution delivers conditioned air through diffusers on the supply side and returns it through grilles. Good distribution mixes air without drafts. Because air must leave a room as fast as it enters, doors and walls need return openings or transfer grilles, and a closed door with no return path pressurizes the room and shortchanges others.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why does a radiant slab need insulation below it, and how does it respond to control changes?

options.A: Insulation sends heat up into the room instead of the soil, and the slab responds slowly, so controls must anticipate
options.B: Insulation prevents the slab from cracking, and the slab responds quickly to changes in thermostat setting
options.C: Insulation protects the tubing from corrosion, and the slab responds instantly to outdoor temperature
options.D: Insulation eliminates the need for a boiler, and the slab responds as quickly as forced air does in the room

questions.explanation: Radiant heating warms surfaces that radiate directly to people and objects, most commonly with warm water in tubing embedded in a slab. It feels comfortable at slightly lower air temperatures because occupants exchange heat with warm surfaces. The thermal mass makes response slow, so controls must anticipate changes in weather.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Net exterior wall of 2,000 ft² has a U-factor of 0.05 and a 60°F temperature difference. What is its conductive heat loss?

options.A: 6,000 BTU/h
options.B: 100 BTU/h
options.D: 600 BTU/h

questions.explanation: Conduction loss is Q = U × A × ΔT = 0.05 × 2,000 × 60 = 6,000 BTU/h. Multiplying only U and area gives 100, and multiplying area by temperature difference gives 120,000. Equipment is sized from loads, never the other way around, and oversizing causes short cycling and poor humidity control. One ton of cooling equals 12,000 BTU/h.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: How do storage, tankless, and heat pump water heaters differ?

options.A: Storage heats on demand with high power, tankless keeps a tank of hot water ready, and a heat pump unit burns fuel oil
options.B: Storage keeps hot water ready and loses heat, tankless heats on demand with high power, and a heat pump unit uses a refrigeration cycle
options.C: Storage and tankless both lose heat all day, and a heat pump water heater needs no electricity at all to run
options.D: Storage uses a refrigeration cycle, tankless uses a tank of hot water, and a heat pump unit uses resistance elements only

questions.explanation: Water for personal use is commonly delivered at about 120°F to limit scalding, and where tanks store water at lower temperatures, designers watch for bacterial growth such as Legionella. Heating 50 gallons from 50°F to 120°F takes about 8.34 × 50 × 70 ≈ 29,200 BTU, from 8.34 lb per gallon and 1 BTU per pound per degree.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: What are detention and infiltration in stormwater management?

options.A: Detention lets water soak into the soil, while infiltration holds it in a basin and releases it slowly
options.B: Detention carries water to the sanitary sewer, while infiltration sends it to the treatment plant
options.C: Detention holds water in a basin and releases it slowly, while infiltration lets it soak into the soil
options.D: Detention speeds runoff off the site, while infiltration collects it on the roof for the building to use

questions.explanation: A developed site produces more runoff, faster, than natural ground, so regulations commonly require a development to release water no faster than before construction. Green roofs also help, and infiltration depends on the site's soil. Stormwater drains are separate from sanitary drains in most modern systems, so rainwater does not overload the treatment plant.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: A sprinkler system serves an unheated loading dock in Minnesota. Which type fits, and why?

options.A: A wet-pipe system, because water in the pipes at all times responds fastest to any fire in the area
options.B: A wet-pipe system, because it is the most common type and therefore is always required by the code
options.C: A dry-pipe system, because it holds water at all times in the pipes and has no air in them at all
options.D: A dry-pipe system, because pressurized air in the pipes prevents freezing until a sprinkler opens

questions.explanation: Sprinkler heads open independently when a glass bulb or link reaches its rated temperature, commonly around 155°F, so only sprinklers near the fire open. Wet-pipe systems hold water at all times and are most common, but water in unheated spaces would freeze. Dry-pipe systems hold pressurized air and admit water only when a sprinkler opens. Flow follows Q = K√P.

questions.chapter: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
questions.question_text: Why are ordinary HVAC fans commonly shut down on a fire alarm while stair pressurization fans operate?

options.A: HVAC fans consume too much electricity during an alarm, while pressurized stairs use stored power
options.B: HVAC fans could spread smoke through the building, while pressurized stairs keep smoke out of exit paths
options.C: HVAC fans produce flames when they run for long periods, while pressurized stairs absorb the smoke
options.D: HVAC fans must be off for the sprinklers to work, while stairs do not need any airflow at all

questions.explanation: Smoke, not flame, is the leading cause of fire deaths because it blocks vision and carries toxic gases. Smoke barriers and dampers limit movement passively, while stair pressurization supplies air so the stair is at higher pressure than the fire floor, and smoke exhaust serves large spaces such as atria. HVAC controls and the fire alarm are one coordinated design tested during commissioning.

questions.question_text: Why does unplugging one computer in a classroom not darken the room's lights?

options.A: Buildings are wired in series, so the current continues through the remaining loads even when one is removed
options.B: Computers are low-voltage devices, so they are not on the same circuit as the lights in the room
options.C: Buildings are wired in parallel, so each device has its own loop and receives the full supply voltage
options.D: The source supplies charge only to the largest load, so the smaller loads are independent of it

questions.explanation: An electrical circuit is a closed path of a source, conductors, and a load, and charge moves only when the loop is complete. In series, one break stops every load, as in old strings of holiday lights. In parallel, each load is on its own path directly across the source, so a break in one path leaves the others complete. Every outlet and light in a classroom is such a separate path.

questions.question_text: What is the correct order of the path electricity follows from the utility into a building?

options.A: Utility service, panelboards, service entrance, feeders, branch circuits
options.B: Service entrance, utility service, branch circuits, panelboards, feeders
options.C: Branch circuits, feeders, panelboards, service entrance, utility service
options.D: Utility service, service entrance, feeders, panelboards, branch circuits

questions.explanation: An electrical system receives electricity from a source, distributes it safely, protects people and property from faults, and delivers it to loads. At each level the current is divided among more paths and the protective devices become smaller. The route in the Riverbend example has six stages: utility line, utility transformer, service entrance, feeder, panelboard, and branch circuit.

questions.question_text: Three parallel circuits fed from one supply draw 10 A, 6 A, and 4 A. What current does the supply conductor carry when all are on?
questions.explanation: In a parallel circuit, the current in the supply conductor is the sum of the branch currents: 10 + 6 + 4 = 20 A. The average, 6.7 A, would understate the load, 10 A counts only the largest branch, and 240 is the product. The same additive idea applies at every level of the building, so feeders are larger than any single branch circuit.

questions.question_text: A utility delivers the same power through a line, but raises the transmission voltage tenfold. What happens to the power lost in the line's resistance?

options.A: It falls to one hundredth, because current falls tenfold and loss depends on the square of current
options.B: It falls to one tenth, because the loss in the line depends directly on the current in the line
options.C: It rises tenfold, because higher voltage forces ten times more power through the same wire
options.D: It stays the same, because the wire's resistance does not change when the voltage is raised

questions.explanation: For a given power, higher voltage needs less current (I = P / V), and wire loss is I²R. At 1,000 V, 100 kW needs 100 A and loses 10,000 W in a 1 ohm line, while at 10,000 V it needs 10 A and loses 100 W. This is why AC dominates: a transformer can change its voltage easily, so transmission lines run at tens or hundreds of thousands of volts.

questions.question_text: At schematic design, a 10,000 ft² building is estimated at 6 VA per square foot on a 208 V three-phase service. About what current does the estimate imply?

options.A: About 288 A
options.B: About 72 A
options.C: About 500 A
options.D: About 167 A

questions.explanation: The demand is 10,000 × 6 = 60,000 VA. Three-phase current is I = VA / (√3 × V) = 60,000 / (1.732 × 208) ≈ 167 A. Omitting the √3 gives 288 A, using 480 V gives about 72 A, and 500 A is unrelated. The designer shares such a rough estimate with the utility early because service requests, transformer purchase, and trenching can take months.

questions.question_text: Which statement about voltage is correct?

options.A: It is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a conductor, measured in amperes or amps
options.B: It is the difference in electrical potential energy per unit of charge between two points, in volts
options.C: It is the opposition that a material offers to the flow of current, measured in ohms at the wire
options.D: It is the rate at which electrical energy is converted into another form, measured in watts

questions.explanation: Voltage is the push that drives charge around a circuit, always measured between two points, like water pressure measured as a difference. Residential outlets are nominally 120 V, large appliances use 240 V, and commercial systems commonly use 208 V or 480 V, with 120 V or 277 V for lighting and receptacles. Low-voltage systems, typically 50 V or less, power doorbells, thermostats, and data cables.

questions.question_text: Why do large commercial buildings typically choose a 480Y/277 V service and use transformers to produce 208Y/120 V for plug loads?

options.A: The higher voltage reduces the power the building uses, so the utility bill is smaller each month and year
options.B: The higher voltage lets the service disconnect be omitted, so the equipment is simpler and cheaper to buy
options.C: The higher voltage reduces the current for a given load, so conductors and equipment are smaller and drop is lower
options.D: The higher voltage is safer to touch, so the equipment needs no protective devices or enclosures

questions.explanation: A 300 kVA load draws about 833 A at 208 V and about 361 A at 480 V, so a 400 A service replaces a 1,000 A one. The service entrance includes the service conductors, meter, service disconnect, and grounding electrode connection, and it sets the capacity of the whole building. Equipment rooms must include clear working space in front of the equipment.

questions.question_text: A three-phase panel carries 2,700 VA on phase A, 1,800 VA on phase B, and 2,200 VA on phase C. Which change best balances the load?

options.A: Move about 450 VA from phase A to phase B
options.B: Move about 450 VA from phase B to phase A
options.C: Move about 900 VA from phase C to phase B
options.D: Move the neutral conductor to phase A

questions.explanation: The total is 6,700 VA, so the average is about 2,233 VA per phase. Moving 450 VA from A to B gives 2,250, 2,250, and 2,200 VA, nearly balanced. The reverse widens the gap, and moving 900 VA from C to B overloads B. Balanced phases reduce neutral current, heating, and voltage differences. A panel schedule lists each circuit, breaker size, equipment, and phase load.

questions.question_text: A circuit's wire has a loop resistance of 0.4 ohms and carries 15 A. How much power is lost as heat in the wire?

options.A: 6 W

questions.explanation: Wire heating follows P = I²R = 15² × 0.4 = 90 W. Using P = I × R gives 6 W, which forgets to square the current, and 225 W omits the resistance. The key insight is that doubling the current makes four times as much heat in the same wire. A building wire is deliberately a low-resistance conductor, and any heat it makes is a loss.

questions.question_text: A continuous load of 2,160 W at 120 V (18 A) is placed on a 20 A circuit. Is this acceptable?

options.A: No, because a continuous load is limited to 80 percent of the breaker rating, 16 A, which 18 A exceeds
options.B: Yes, because 18 A is below the 20 A rating, so the breaker will not trip during normal use
options.C: Yes, because the wire is 12 AWG, which can carry any load below 30 A without overheating
options.D: No, because a 20 A circuit can serve only loads that run for less than one hour at a time

questions.explanation: The code treats a load running three hours or more as continuous, and the breaker rating must exceed the load current by 25 percent, which is equivalent to using no more than 80 percent of the rating. For a 20 A breaker that is 16 A. A breaker protects the wire, not people, and should never be replaced with a larger one to stop it from tripping.

questions.question_text: A long 12 AWG branch circuit shows a voltage drop of about 6 percent. What is the usual remedy, and why does it work?

options.A: Use a smaller conductor with a larger AWG number, which raises the resistance and lowers the current
options.B: Use a higher-rated breaker, which increases the voltage available at the load end of the circuit
options.C: Use a larger conductor with a smaller AWG number, which lowers the resistance and the voltage drop
options.D: Use a longer conductor, which spreads the current over a greater length and reduces heating

questions.explanation: Resistance is the opposition to current, caused by electrons colliding with atoms. It depends on material and geometry: longer wire has more resistance and thicker wire has less. A smaller gauge number means a thicker wire, and every three gauge steps roughly halves resistance. Moving to 10 AWG reduces the 100 ft example's drop from about 7.7 V to about 4.8 V.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a typical source or use of direct current in a building?

options.A: The utility service from the street, which is delivered to buildings at 60 hertz as direct current
options.B: The secondary of a transformer, which only works when the supplied current is steady and direct
options.C: A motor on a three-phase supply, which requires the polarity to reverse many times each second
options.D: Batteries for emergency lighting, photovoltaic arrays, and the output of electronic power supplies

questions.explanation: In DC the voltage is steady and polarity never changes, so Ohm's law applies directly and connecting a device backward can damage it. Many electronics, including LED drivers, computers, and phones, use DC internally even when plugged into an AC outlet. Utility power is AC because its voltage can be changed efficiently by a transformer, which works only with alternating current.

questions.question_text: How are wire gauge and breaker rating matched in typical branch circuits?

options.A: A 15 A circuit uses 12 AWG wire and a 20 A circuit uses 14 AWG wire
options.B: A 15 A circuit uses 14 AWG wire and a 20 A circuit uses 12 AWG wire
options.C: A 15 A circuit uses 10 AWG wire and a 20 A circuit uses 8 AWG wire
options.D: A 15 A circuit and a 20 A circuit both use 14 AWG wire

questions.explanation: A branch circuit is the wiring between the final overcurrent device and the outlets, lights, or equipment it serves. Most are 15 or 20 A at 120 V. A typical cable contains a hot conductor that carries current to the load, a neutral that carries it back, and a ground that stays dead and provides a safe path for fault current. Thicker wire has a smaller AWG number.

questions.question_text: Why is switchgear found in hospitals and data centers instead of a simpler switchboard?

options.A: Its breakers are smaller and lighter, so it fits in tighter equipment rooms at the service entrance
options.B: Its breakers do not need an interrupting rating, so they are less costly to buy and to install
options.C: Its breakers are fused instead of tripped, so they never need to be reset after a fault occurs
options.D: Its breakers are on draw-out rails, so one can be removed for maintenance without shutting down the building

questions.explanation: Switchgear is a metal-enclosed assembly of main breakers, switches, busbars, and controls at the service entrance of a large building. A switchboard is simpler and less costly, and common in mid-size buildings. Both must be rated for the available fault current, the large current that would flow in a short circuit at that point, which the utility helps determine.

questions.question_text: What does a feeder do, and how is it sized?

options.A: It carries power from a panelboard to a single outlet, and it is sized for the one device it serves
options.B: It carries power from the utility pole to the street transformer, and it is sized by the utility
options.C: It carries power from service equipment to a panelboard, and it is sized for the sum of the downstream loads
options.D: It carries ground fault current to the earth, and it is sized for the largest breaker in the system

questions.explanation: Feeders connect the levels of the electrical system, such as a main switchboard to a lighting panelboard or a transformer. They are sized for everything downstream, which is why feeder wires are much larger than branch-circuit wires. Informational notes in the code suggest keeping voltage drop to about 3 percent on a feeder and about 5 percent from the service to the farthest load.

questions.question_text: Why do commercial customers pay both for energy in kilowatt-hours and for demand in kilowatts?

options.A: Energy is total work done over time, while demand is the highest rate of use, so many large loads at once cost more
options.B: Energy is the highest rate of use in a billing period, while demand is the total work done, so both measure the same quantity
options.C: Energy is the rate at which a load runs, while demand is the voltage of the supply to the building
options.D: Energy measures the cost of wire loss in the building, while demand measures the cost of the transformers

questions.explanation: Power is the rate at which energy is converted, in watts, and energy equals power times time. A 1,500 W heater running 8 hours uses 12 kWh. A utility bill's demand charge penalizes peaks, so designers and operators schedule and control equipment to flatten them. Power and energy are different, much as speed and distance are different.

questions.question_text: A 150 kVA transformer steps 480 V down to 208 V, carrying about 180 A on the primary side and 416 A on the secondary side. Why is the secondary current higher?

options.A: A transformer adds power on the secondary side, so both the voltage and the current increase on that side
options.B: A transformer converts AC to DC on the secondary side, which raises the current delivered to the load
options.C: A transformer creates no power, so power in nearly equals power out, and a lower voltage means a higher current
options.D: A transformer's turns ratio sets current equal on both sides, so the difference comes from wire resistance

questions.explanation: A transformer changes the voltage of AC using two coils sharing a magnetic core. A changing current in the primary induces a voltage in the secondary, and the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. It works only with AC. The losses appear as heat, so transformers need ventilation and clearance. Utilities use pad-mounted units outside, and buildings use dry-type units indoors.

questions.chapter: Electrical Distribution, Lighting, and Design Team Coordination
questions.question_text: Lighting expected to run continuously has a connected load of 8,000 VA. At what value should the equipment feeding it be sized?

options.A: 6,400 VA, which is 80 percent of the continuous load
options.B: 10,000 VA, which is 125 percent of the continuous load
options.C: 8,000 VA, which is the connected load
options.D: 1,000 VA, which is the demand factor

questions.explanation: A continuous load is any load expected to run for three hours or more, and the code requires equipment feeding it to be sized at 125 percent, the 80 percent rule seen from the other side. So 8,000 × 1.25 = 10,000 VA. The connected load is the sum of nameplate ratings as if everything ran at once, while the demand load is what the system is expected to carry at its peak.

questions.chapter: Electrical Distribution, Lighting, and Design Team Coordination
